C. Observation is right for asymptomatic bacteriuria in non-pregnant patients, but in pregnancy it must be treated because of the risk of pyelonephritis and preterm birth.
key_concept:
Asymptomatic bacteriuria: treat only in pregnancy (and before urological procedures, renal transplant).
  • Screen with urine culture at the first antenatal visit
  • Treat per sensitivity: amoxicillin, cephalexin are safe options
  • Nitrofurantoin: avoid in the third trimester / near term
  • Avoid: tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones; aminoglycosides not first line (reserved for severe infection)
  • Repeat culture after treatment (test of cure)
exam_pearl: Same culture in a non-pregnant woman = observe; pregnant = treat.

stem: Female pregnant at 28 experienced vaginal discharge and cramps «she has a history of pregnancy loss or preterm labor I don't remember exactly» and the doctor considered about this pregnancy, what is the best to do for good outcome ?
OptB: Go and monitor herself and came in if she is in pain or in severe pain
highlight_terms_source: history of pregnancy loss or preterm labor
why_right: The doctor is concerned because of a history of pregnancy loss or preterm labor; a prior spontaneous preterm birth is the strongest risk factor for recurrence. Progesterone, given as indicated, is the recognised measure that reduces recurrent preterm birth in such women, so it is the only listed option aimed at a good outcome.
why_wrong_block:
A. Muscle-strengthening exercise has no role in preventing preterm birth; it is general advice, not a targeted intervention.
B. Sending a high-risk woman with cramps and discharge home to self-monitor is unsafe; symptoms at 28 weeks need assessment for preterm labor (cervical exam), not delayed presentation.
key_concept:
Preventing preterm birth in high-risk women.
  • Prior spontaneous preterm birth: progesterone, started in the second trimester
  • Short cervix on transvaginal scan (<25 mm): vaginal progesterone; cerclage if prior mid-trimester loss
  • Strict bed rest and aspirin do not prevent preterm birth
  • Symptomatic (contractions + cervical change): steroids, tocolysis, MgSO4 per gestation
exam_pearl: Progesterone prevents preterm birth in at-risk women; it does not treat established preterm labor.

stem: Young lady (27y i think) newly married presented to the ER with sever RLQ abdominal pain associated with vaginal spotting blood. No fever or nausea or vomiting (100% sure there's no fever but not sure if there N&V or no) on EXAMINATION there is RLQ tenderness. What is the preliminary appropriate test/tests ( ?)
OptC: cbc, pregnancy test and urine analysis
why_right: A newly married woman with RLQ pain and vaginal spotting needs ectopic pregnancy excluded first, while appendicitis, UTI or stone, and torsion remain possible. The lead-in asks for the preliminary tests: a pregnancy test decides the whole pathway, CBC looks for blood loss or leukocytosis, and urinalysis screens for urinary causes, all quick bedside steps before imaging.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ultrasound is the next step, chosen and interpreted according to the pregnancy test (transvaginal if hCG positive); it is not the first test when pregnancy status is unknown.
B. Option not recalled; any preliminary set without a pregnancy test (for example CT first, or observation) would be wrong in a woman of reproductive age with pain and spotting.
D. CBC and renal function omit the pregnancy test, the single most important result in a reproductive-age woman with pain and bleeding; renal function adds little here.
key_concept:
Woman of reproductive age + abdominal pain: pregnancy test first.
  • Initial: beta-hCG (urine/serum), CBC, urinalysis
  • hCG positive: transvaginal ultrasound (ectopic vs intrauterine)
  • hCG negative: ultrasound for torsion, appendicitis, ovarian cyst
  • Pregnancy must be excluded before any CT
  • Unstable: resuscitate and treat as ruptured ectopic
exam_pearl: Pain + spotting in a newly married woman is ectopic until hCG says otherwise; labs before scan.

stem: A 20 week pregnancy came to antenatal care , she doesn't have any Complaint medically free and no family history of GDM What is the most appropriate ?
OptC: Give low dose aspirin to prevent preeclampsia
OptD: Give iron supplements to prevent anemia
why_right: She is a low-risk woman at 20 weeks with no complaints, medically free and no GDM risk. None of the risk-triggered tests or drugs apply, so the appropriate routine measure is iron supplementation to prevent the anemia of pregnancy, as rising demand peaks in the second and third trimesters.
why_wrong_block:
A. A 24 hour urine protein is done to quantify proteinuria when hypertension or preeclampsia is suspected after 20 weeks; she is normotensive and asymptomatic.
B. Early GDM screening is for risk factors such as previous GDM or obesity; with no risk she is screened routinely at 24 to 28 weeks.
C. Low dose aspirin is for women with preeclampsia risk factors and is ideally started before 16 weeks; she has neither the indication nor the timing.
key_concept:
Low-risk 20-week visit: routine care only.
  • Iron (with folic acid) supplementation to prevent anemia
  • OGTT at 24 to 28 weeks; early only with risk factors
  • Aspirin only for preeclampsia risk factors, started early
  • Proteinuria workup only if BP ≥140/90 after 20 weeks
  • Anatomy scan around 18 to 22 weeks
exam_pearl: "Medically free, no complaints, no family history" removes every risk-based option; choose the routine supplement.

stem: 50 yr female c/o menorrhagia for one year, medical management has failed. US shows a fibroid 7x7 cm Most appropriate management:
why_right: Two surgical indications are present: a 7x7 cm fibroid (large) and failed medical management of a year of menorrhagia. At 50 years fertility preservation is not needed, so the definitive surgical option, hysterectomy, is most appropriate (myomectomy would be chosen only to preserve fertility).
why_wrong_block:
B. Uterine artery embolization is for a surgical candidate who declines surgery; nothing in the stem says she refuses.
C. A hormonal IUD is medical treatment, which has already failed, and a 7 cm fibroid can distort the cavity, making placement and retention unreliable.
D. Oral progesterone is also medical treatment; it will not control a 7 cm fibroid after medical therapy has failed.
key_concept:
Fibroid with menorrhagia: escalate by indication.
  • Medical first: NSAIDs, tranexamic acid, OCP, progestins, LNG-IUD
  • Surgery if large (>7 cm) or medical failure
  • Family complete or older: hysterectomy
  • Wants fertility: myomectomy
  • Refuses surgery: uterine artery embolization
exam_pearl: Same fibroid in a woman who refuses surgery = embolization; in a woman wanting pregnancy = myomectomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Numbered 1099. A fuller 'Q:' variant (fibroid distorting the endometrial lining; options include endometrial ablation) is carded separately.

stem: A 50-year-old woman presents with menorrhagia for the last year. The physical examination is unremarkable. A trial of medical treatment failed to control the bleeding for the last few months. Ultrasound: Presence of a fibroid, 7 x 7 cm in size, which is distorting the endometrial lining. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Two surgical triggers are present: a 7 x 7 cm fibroid and failed medical treatment for persistent menorrhagia. At 50 years fertility preservation is not a goal, so definitive surgery (hysterectomy) is preferred over myomectomy or uterus-sparing measures; it removes the fibroid and stops the bleeding permanently.
why_wrong_block:
B. Endometrial ablation treats heavy bleeding from a normal-shaped cavity; a large fibroid distorting the endometrial lining makes ablation ineffective and technically unsuitable.
C. Uterine artery embolization is the alternative for a surgical candidate who declines or is unfit for surgery; nothing here says she refuses hysterectomy.
D. A hormonal IUD is a medical option and medical therapy has already failed; a distorted cavity also makes placement and retention unreliable. It suits menorrhagia with a normal cavity.
key_concept:
Fibroid ladder: asymptomatic = observe; symptomatic = medical; large or failed medical = surgery.
  • Incidental, asymptomatic: observation with follow-up ultrasound
  • Symptomatic: medical therapy first (e.g. OCP); GnRH agonist preoperatively to shrink
  • Surgery indications: large fibroid or failed medical treatment
  • Fertility wanted: myomectomy (hysteroscopic if submucosal)
  • Family complete / older: hysterectomy
  • Refuses surgery: uterine artery embolization
exam_pearl: Same fibroid in a woman who wants children points to myomectomy; refusal of surgery points to embolization.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Unnumbered 'Q:' variant printed under 1099 with 'Answer: A'.

stem: 33-year-old single woman was found to have a uterine fibroid incidentally on pelvic ultrasound. Ultrasound: Subserosal uterine fibroid measuring 5x5 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
key_concept:
Fibroid ladder: asymptomatic = observe; symptomatic = medical; failed or large = surgery.
  • Incidental, asymptomatic: conservative, yearly ultrasound
  • Bleeding: OCP / medical; GnRH agonist pre-op to shrink
  • Surgery: large, pressure symptoms, infertility, or failed medical therapy
  • Myomectomy if fertility wanted; hysterectomy if family complete
  • UAE: refuses surgery
  • A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Conservative.
exam_pearl: Decide by symptoms, not by the fibroid: no symptoms = observe; heavy bleeding = medical first; surgical indication = myomectomy if fertility wanted.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with severe generalized abdominal pain, associated with nausea and vomiting for the last few hours. She is known to have an intrauterine contraceptive device inserted for the last 3 years. She did a home pregnancy test, which was positive. Ultrasound: Fluid collection of approximately 13 x 15 cm. No identified gestational sac. Both ovaries are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
highlight_terms_source: Fluid collection of approximately 13 x 15 cm
why_right: A "positive" pregnancy test with "no identified gestational sac" in the uterus suggests an ectopic pregnancy, and an IUD in situ makes any pregnancy that does occur proportionally more likely to be ectopic. "Severe generalized abdominal pain" with a large "13 x 15 cm" fluid collection indicates haemoperitoneum, meaning the ectopic has ruptured. "Both ovaries are normal" argues against an ovarian source of bleeding.
why_wrong_block:
A. A ruptured corpus luteum can bleed into the peritoneum, but the ovaries are reported normal, and with a positive test and no intrauterine sac a ruptured ectopic must be assumed.
B. An intact ectopic causes localized pain with little or no free fluid; a huge fluid collection and generalized pain mean rupture.
D. An early intrauterine pregnancy would not explain severe generalized pain with massive free fluid and no intrauterine sac.
key_concept:
Positive hCG + empty uterus + free fluid = ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise.
  • No intrauterine sac with hCG above the discriminatory zone (about 1500 to 2000): suspect ectopic
  • Adnexal mass without free fluid: intact ectopic
  • Large free fluid, generalized pain, shoulder tip pain or shock: ruptured
  • IUD failure: pregnancy more likely ectopic
  • Ruptured or unstable: surgery, not methotrexate
exam_pearl: An IUD lowers overall pregnancy risk, but if a pregnancy occurs with one in place, think ectopic first.

stem: A 31-weeks pregnant woman presents with ROM the fluid is clear Nitrazine test is positive, CTG is reassuring What is the most preventive measure ( i am not sure ) ?
why_right: Clear fluid with a positive nitrazine test at 31 weeks is PPROM. With a reassuring CTG and no sign of infection, management is expectant: antibiotics (ampicillin plus erythromycin) to prevent chorioamnionitis and prolong latency, and corticosteroids because she is under 34 weeks. These are the measures that actually prevent maternal and neonatal harm.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tocolysis is not recommended once membranes have ruptured; it does not improve outcome and may mask infection. Tocolytics plus steroids fit preterm labor with intact membranes.
B. Delivery is indicated in PPROM only for chorioamnionitis, abruption, non-reassuring CTG or cord prolapse risk, or at 34 weeks and beyond; at 31 weeks with a reassuring CTG it adds prematurity without benefit.
key_concept:
PPROM: steroids, antibiotics, MgSO4 by gestation; deliver only for a reason.
  • <32 weeks: MgSO4 (fetal neuroprotection)
  • <34 weeks: antenatal corticosteroids
  • Antibiotics: ampicillin + erythromycin
  • Deliver: chorioamnionitis, abruption, non-reassuring CTG, cord prolapse risk
  • No tocolysis after rupture of membranes
exam_pearl: Intact membranes in preterm labor = tocolytic + steroid; ruptured membranes = antibiotic + steroid, no tocolytic.

stem: A 28-year-old G1 P0 woman presented to the Emergency Room at 30 weeks gestation with abdominal pain with no leaking or bleeding. The CTG shows a normal heart rate with regular contractions 4 in 10 minutes. She was admitted with preterm labor, as her cervix was 2 cm dilated and 80% effaced. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptD: This is a threatened preterm labor, so observation
highlight_terms_source: cervix was 2 cm dilated and 80% effaced
why_right: "Regular contractions 4 in 10 minutes" with the cervix "2 cm dilated and 80% effaced" at 30 weeks is established preterm labor, not threatened. Below 34 weeks she needs dexamethasone for fetal lung maturity, a tocolytic (nifedipine) to delay delivery long enough for the steroid to work, and GBS prophylaxis because delivery may be imminent. This option is the only one that covers the full bundle.
why_wrong_block:
A. Informing NICU is reasonable, but simply anticipating delivery gives no steroids or tocolysis and wastes the chance to improve fetal lung maturity.
B. Incomplete: without a tocolytic, delivery may occur before the steroid course reaches its benefit.
D. Threatened preterm labor means contractions without cervical change; she has cervical dilation and effacement, so observation is wrong.
key_concept:
Preterm labor <34 weeks: steroids + tocolytic + GBS prophylaxis (+ MgSO4 if <32 weeks).
  • Preterm labor = regular contractions + cervical change before 37 weeks
  • Steroids <34 weeks: lung maturity
  • MgSO4 <32 weeks: fetal neuroprotection
  • Tocolysis buys time for steroids; not used once in active labor
  • >34 weeks: proceed to delivery
exam_pearl: Contractions without cervical change = threatened (observe); with cervical change = preterm labor (treat). At 30 weeks MgSO4 for neuroprotection would also be given, though it is not listed.

stem: A 35-year-old G9 P6026 at 8 weeks' gestation presents to the hospital with vaginal spotting associated with very mild lower abdominal pain. She has noticed some dark brown clots. Examination reveals she is comfortable in bed with no abdominal tenderness appreciated. Transvaginal ultrasound: 5-week gestational size with no fetal heart. Pelvic examination reveals minimal dark-red clots in the introitus and cervical os closed Which of the following is the most appropriate next step of management plan?
highlight_terms_source: 5-week gestational size with no fetal heart
why_right: She is 8 weeks by dates but the scan shows a 5-week size with no fetal heart, with a closed os and only minimal dark clots: a non-viable pregnancy that has not been expelled, i.e. missed abortion. She is comfortable, stable and has no signs of infection, and in the first trimester (under 13 weeks) expectant management is an appropriate first option.
why_wrong_block:
A. Suction curettage is for heavy bleeding, hemodynamic instability, infection, failed expectant or medical management, or patient preference; none apply here.
B. The prostaglandin used for medical management of miscarriage is misoprostol (PGE1); PGE2 is a cervical ripening agent for induction of labor, and expectant management is acceptable first.
D. There is no fever, tenderness or foul discharge, so antibiotics (septic abortion management) are not indicated.
key_concept:
Abortion types by os and tissue.
  • Threatened: closed os, viable fetus: reassurance
  • Missed: closed os, non-viable, no tissue passed: expectant (<13 weeks), misoprostol, or evacuation
  • Inevitable: open os, no tissue passed
  • Incomplete: open os, partial tissue passed: evacuation
  • Complete: closed os, empty uterus: follow-up
  • Septic: fever, tenderness, foul discharge: antibiotics + evacuation
exam_pearl: Closed os + no fetal heart + stable patient in the first trimester = expectant management first.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' variant (40-year-old G9 P6026 at 9 weeks, 5-week gestational size, no fetal heart): options Misoprostol / Mifepristone / Dilatation and curettage / Conservative management; Conservative management highlighted (consistent).

stem: What is the maternal risk factor for post term delivery .
why_right: The question asks for the maternal risk carried by a post-term pregnancy. Prolonged pregnancy raises the rate of cesarean section (larger baby, failed induction, labor dystocia and fetal distress), together with perineal trauma and postpartum hemorrhage. Cesarean delivery is the classic maternal consequence among these options.
why_wrong_block:
A. Anesthesia is a consequence of an operative delivery, not a recognized independent maternal risk of going post-term.
B. Blood transfusion may follow a hemorrhage but is not a listed maternal risk of post-term pregnancy in itself.
C. Placenta previa is a cause of antepartum bleeding and is delivered by elective cesarean at 36 to 37 weeks; it is linked to early, not post-term, delivery.
key_concept:
Post-term (≥42 weeks): risks to mother and fetus rise, so induction is offered from 41 weeks.
  • Maternal: cesarean delivery, operative vaginal delivery, perineal trauma, PPH
  • Fetal: macrosomia, oligohydramnios, meconium aspiration, stillbirth
  • 41 weeks not in labor: induction of labor
exam_pearl: Read "maternal risk" as the complication the mother faces from going overdue: more cesarean sections.

stem: Delivered baby delayed placental for 30min What's the most appropriate
why_right: Placenta not delivered 30 minutes after the baby is a retained placenta. Of the drugs offered, oxytocin is the first-line uterotonic and the one used in third-stage management to encourage separation and limit bleeding while manual removal is arranged.
why_wrong_block:
A. Misoprostol is a second-line uterotonic (useful for atonic PPH when oxytocin is unavailable); it has not been shown to help deliver a retained placenta.
B. Carboprost is a later-line drug for atonic PPH (contraindicated in asthma); it is not used to expel a retained placenta.
key_concept:
Retained placenta = not delivered by 30 minutes after the baby.
  • Wait 30 minutes with active management (oxytocin, controlled cord traction)
  • Still retained: manual removal under anesthesia + antibiotics
  • Fails or tissue left: dilatation and curettage
  • Adherent at removal: think accreta
exam_pearl: If "manual removal of the placenta" is offered, it beats any drug at 30 minutes.

stem: Which vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy?
why_right: HPV vaccine is the only option not given during pregnancy: it is not live, but safety data are limited, so it is deferred until after delivery (and an interrupted series is completed postpartum). Whooping cough (Tdap), influenza and COVID vaccines are all actively recommended in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tdap is recommended in every pregnancy, at 27 to 36 weeks, so maternal antibodies protect the newborn from pertussis.
B. Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended in any trimester because flu is more severe in pregnancy; only the live intranasal form is avoided.
D. COVID vaccination is recommended in pregnancy because infection carries higher maternal and fetal risk.
key_concept:
Pregnancy vaccines: give inactivated, avoid live, defer HPV.
  • Give: Tdap (27 to 36 weeks), inactivated flu, COVID
  • Contraindicated (live): MMR/rubella, varicella, live zoster
  • Defer: HPV (not live, limited data)
  • Rubella and varicella: give preconception
exam_pearl: If a live vaccine (varicella, MMR) is listed, it beats HPV as the contraindicated one.

stem: Which vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy?
why_right: "VSV" is a recall typo for VZV, the varicella vaccine, a live attenuated vaccine. Live vaccines are contraindicated in pregnancy because of the theoretical risk of fetal infection, so varicella is the true contraindication here. Non-immune women are vaccinated before conception or after delivery.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tdap (whooping cough) is recommended in every pregnancy at 27 to 36 weeks to protect the newborn.
B. Inactivated influenza vaccine is recommended in pregnancy in any trimester.
C. HPV is not live; it is deferred until after pregnancy because of limited data, not truly contraindicated. It becomes the answer only in the variant where no live vaccine is listed.
key_concept:
Live vaccine in the options = the contraindicated one.
  • Live (avoid): varicella, MMR/rubella, live zoster, smallpox
  • Defer: HPV
  • Give: Tdap, inactivated flu, COVID
  • Varicella or rubella non-immune: vaccinate preconception or postpartum
exam_pearl: Same stem, different options: with varicella listed pick varicella; without it, pick HPV.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Typed version highlights VSV (likely VZV/varicella). 'Q:' variant: A 24 years old newly married came to preconception visit, which vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy? Flu vaccine / Covid / Whooping / HPV, with HPV highlighted (HPV not among options of the typed version as highlighted answer).
Other marked answers: 'Q:' restatement (24 y newly married, preconception visit; Flu/Covid/Whooping/HPV): HPV highlighted

stem: A case of female patient had severe pain before and during her menstrual cycle Which made her absent few days and that's made her boss unhappy :) What to give her?
highlight_terms_source: severe pain before and during her menstrual cycle
key_concept:
Primary dysmenorrhea: NSAIDs first, combined OCP next (or first if contraception wanted).
  • Pain starting just before or with menses, normal exam
  • Step 1: NSAIDs (anti-prostaglandin)
  • Step 2: combined OCP
  • Paracetamol: weaker fallback
  • Never a prostaglandin (misoprostol)
  • A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Combined hormonal contraceptive pills (not among these recalled options).
exam_pearl: Misoprostol is a prostaglandin; prostaglandins are the cause of dysmenorrhea pain.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Young woman with severe abdominal pain one day before menses and two days after which stops her from going to work and boss is not happy about it!
highlight_terms_source: severe abdominal pain one day before menses and two days after
stops her from going to work
why_right: Severe pain from one day before menses lasting into the first days, bad enough to miss work, in a young woman is primary dysmenorrhea. NSAIDs are not offered, so the effective choice is the combined OCP, which suppresses ovulation and endometrial prostaglandin production.
why_wrong_block:
A. Acetaminophen has no anti-prostaglandin effect, so it is a weak option for severe, work-limiting dysmenorrhea; acceptable only for mild pain or when other drugs are contraindicated.
C. Progestin-only pills are not the standard treatment for primary dysmenorrhea; they suit women needing contraception with a contraindication to estrogen.
key_concept:
Primary dysmenorrhea ladder.
  • Step 1: NSAIDs
  • Step 2 (or first if contraception wanted): combined OCP
  • No NSAID in options: choose combined OCP
  • Abnormal exam or no response: look for secondary cause (endometriosis, adenomyosis)
exam_pearl: If NSAIDs are listed, they are the first step; missing work does not skip them.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' variant: severe dysmenorrhea starting one day before menses and continuing up to 3 days, prevents attending work; asking about management: Paracetamol / OCP (highlighted). (No mention for NSAIDs)

stem: 30 year old 9week pregnant came with mild vaginal bleeding and mild abdominal pain Cervix open B HCG: 3000 US: no intrauterine or extrauterine product of conception Whats most apropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: no intrauterine or extrauterine product of conception
why_right: At 9 weeks with β-hCG 3000 and no intrauterine pregnancy on ultrasound, an ectopic pregnancy is presumed (hCG is above the level at which an intrauterine sac should be seen). She is stable with only mild pain and bleeding, no visible mass or rupture, and hCG is low, so she meets criteria for medical treatment with methotrexate.
why_wrong_block:
B. Salpingectomy is for a ruptured or unstable ectopic, a large mass, contraindication to methotrexate, or failed medical treatment; none applies here.
C. Salpingostomy is also surgery, chosen at laparoscopy to preserve the tube (needs hCG follow-up); it is not first choice when methotrexate criteria are met.
D. D&C evacuates intrauterine tissue in miscarriage; the uterus is empty and does not treat an ectopic.
key_concept:
Stable ectopic with low hCG = methotrexate; unstable or failed = surgery.
  • MTX: stable, unruptured, hCG ≤5000, mass <4 cm, no fetal heart
  • Surgery: unstable, ruptured, failed MTX, contraindication
  • Salpingectomy: removes tube; salpingostomy: keeps tube, follow hCG
  • Stable PUL below discriminatory level: repeat hCG and US in 48 h
exam_pearl: Severe pain, rebound or instability flips the answer from methotrexate to surgery.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Q:' variant (next page): 33-year-old at 9 weeks with mild vaginal bleeding, mild tenderness, closed cervix, US no intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy; options Salpingotomy / Salpingectomy / Methotrexate injection (highlighted) / Evacuation and curettage.

stem: 38w vaginal delivery after 30 min placenta still not delivered how to manage
why_right: Placenta still in place 30 minutes after a vaginal delivery is a retained placenta. Among the drugs offered, IV oxytocin is the first-line uterotonic: it promotes contraction and limits bleeding while manual removal is prepared. Oxytocin is given IV or IM, never orally.
why_wrong_block:
A. Misoprostol is a second-line uterotonic for atonic PPH; it has not been shown to help deliver a retained placenta.
C. Carboprost is a later-line drug for atonic PPH (avoid in asthma), not a treatment for retained placenta.
D. Ergometrine causes sustained uterine contraction that can close the cervix and trap the placenta; it is also contraindicated in hypertension.
key_concept:
Third stage: oxytocin and cord traction, then manual removal at 30 minutes.
  • Wait 30 minutes after the baby
  • Retained: manual removal under anesthesia + antibiotics
  • Fails or retained tissue: dilatation and curettage
  • Uterotonic order for atony: oxytocin, ergometrine, carboprost, misoprostol
exam_pearl: When "manual removal" is an option at 30 minutes, it is the answer over IV oxytocin.

stem: pregnant i think 30w heart failure ef 30 how to manage main complain dyspnea Calss ll NYHA
why_right: She is pregnant (30 weeks) with systolic heart failure (EF 30%) and only mild symptoms (NYHA class II: dyspnea on ordinary activity). Outside pregnancy an ACE inhibitor or ARB would be the cornerstone, but both are contraindicated in pregnancy. Hydralazine (usually paired with a nitrate) is the pregnancy-safe afterload reducer used in their place, alongside a beta blocker and diuretics as needed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Losartan: an ARB is fetotoxic (fetal renal damage, oligohydramnios) and contraindicated in pregnancy. Right for HFrEF in a non-pregnant patient, or postpartum.
B. Lisinopril: ACE inhibitors carry the same fetal renal toxicity and are contraindicated in pregnancy. It is the standard HFrEF drug outside pregnancy, and is restarted after delivery.
C. Methyldopa: a central antihypertensive used for chronic or mild hypertension in pregnancy; it does not unload the failing ventricle and has no role in treating heart failure.
key_concept:
HFrEF in pregnancy: swap ACEi/ARB for hydralazine (plus nitrate).
  • Contraindicated: ACE inhibitors, ARBs (fetal renal toxicity)
  • Afterload reduction: hydralazine with or without nitrate
  • Beta blocker (e.g. metoprolol) and loop diuretics for congestion can continue
  • Methyldopa, labetalol: antihypertensives, not HF therapy
  • NYHA II: comfortable at rest, symptoms with ordinary activity
exam_pearl: Any "-pril" or "-sartan" in a pregnant patient is wrong; the pregnancy substitute for HF afterload reduction is hydralazine.

stem: Pregnant was referred from maternal something as preterm labour. She has history of ruptured membrane and contraction (did not specify time). She planned for C/S. No vital signs Didn't mention if she has DM. Ask about what is the most imp to be available Before Anesthesia (didn't say time out or sign)
why_right: She is heading to an urgent caesarean for preterm labour with ruptured membranes, and the question asks what must be in place before anaesthesia. In the pre-induction (sign-in) safety check, the key preparation for an obstetric operation is anticipating haemorrhage: a valid group and save or crossmatch with blood available. Caesarean delivery carries a real risk of major blood loss, so blood reserve is the item that cannot be missing.
why_wrong_block:
A. Antibiotics with anaesthesia: prophylactic antibiotics are given before skin incision and confirmed at the time-out step; they matter, but they are not the safety item that must be secured before induction.
B. Blood glucose monitor: relevant only for a diabetic patient or one on insulin; nothing in the stem mentions diabetes.
key_concept:
Before an obstetric operation: plan for bleeding first.
  • Sign-in (before induction): identity, consent, anaesthesia check, airway, allergy, expected blood loss with blood available
  • Time-out (before incision): team confirmation, antibiotic prophylaxis given
  • Sign-out: counts, specimen, recovery plan
  • Caesarean: always group and save or crossmatch beforehand
exam_pearl: "Before anaesthesia" points to the sign-in step, where blood availability is checked; antibiotics belong to the time-out before incision.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot answer line: 'C- blood reserve (OR results) available'.

stem: asthmatic woman during labour experienced bleeding that did not stop with oxytocin and manual massage what is the appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: bleeding that did not stop with oxytocin and manual massage
why_right: This is atonic PPH that persisted after the first steps (oxytocin and uterine massage), so the next move is a second uterotonic. The patient is asthmatic, which rules out carboprost (PGF2 alpha causes bronchospasm). IM methylergonovine is the appropriate next uterotonic, provided she is not hypertensive.
why_wrong_block:
A. IM carboprost: PGF2 alpha is a bronchoconstrictor and is contraindicated in bronchial asthma. It is the right next drug when methylergonovine is barred, e.g. in a hypertensive or preeclamptic woman.
C. Balloon tamponade: the next step after vaginal delivery only once medical (uterotonic) treatment has failed; a second-line uterotonic has not been tried yet.
D. This option is garbled in the recall ("100%", possibly 100% oxygen); oxygen is supportive resuscitation and does not stop atonic bleeding.
key_concept:
Atonic PPH: massage plus uterotonics in order, choosing around contraindications.
  • 1st: oxytocin
  • Methylergonovine: avoid in hypertension or preeclampsia
  • Carboprost (PGF2 alpha): avoid in asthma
  • Misoprostol: no asthma or BP restriction
  • After vaginal delivery, medical failure: balloon tamponade, then embolization (stable) or uterine artery ligation (unstable), then hysterectomy
exam_pearl: Asthma bars carboprost; hypertension bars methylergonovine. Read the comorbidity before choosing the second uterotonic.

stem: Young lady , recently get married, present to the ER with sudden RLQ pain for (1 day ? Not sure) , vomiting 3 times , abdominal tenderness especially in RIQ No wbc in the Q There was another test result but I forget what it was … Next step ?
OptD: I don't remember but maybe colonoscopy
why_right: A young, recently married woman with sudden RLQ pain and vomiting could have a gynaecological emergency (ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion, ruptured or haemorrhagic cyst) as well as appendicitis. The first imaging is a pelvic ultrasound, with a pregnancy test (beta-hCG) alongside it: ultrasound sorts the adnexal causes, can show the appendix, and avoids radiation in a woman who may be pregnant.
why_wrong_block:
B. Abdominal CT: exposes a possibly pregnant woman to radiation and is less suited than ultrasound with Doppler for adnexal causes such as torsion or ectopic pregnancy. Right once pregnancy is excluded and ultrasound is inconclusive, e.g. an obese adult with suspected appendicitis.
C. Diagnostic laparoscopy: invasive; used when imaging is inconclusive and suspicion stays high, or for an unstable patient or strongly suspected torsion needing surgery anyway.
D. Colonoscopy: no role in acute abdominal pain and risks perforation if appendicitis is present; it is for chronic bowel symptoms or bleeding.
key_concept:
Woman of reproductive age with acute lower abdominal pain: rule out pregnancy, then ultrasound.
  • Beta-hCG first in every woman of reproductive age
  • Pelvic or transvaginal US: ectopic, torsion, cyst, also the appendix
  • CT: only after pregnancy is excluded and US is unhelpful
  • Laparoscopy: diagnostic and therapeutic when imaging fails or the patient is unstable
exam_pearl: "Recently married" is the stem's way of saying possible pregnancy: think ectopic or torsion and choose ultrasound over CT.

stem: 15 years old, no menstruation, phenotypical female and BMI less than 5th percentile, what improves her condition?
why_right: A 15-year-old phenotypic female with no menses and BMI below the 5th percentile has functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea from low energy reserves. Too little body fat (low leptin) suppresses GnRH pulsatility, so LH, FSH and oestrogen stay low and menarche is delayed. Restoring weight and body fat is what reactivates the axis and allows menstruation.
why_wrong_block:
B. Exercise: more energy expenditure worsens the deficit; excessive exercise is itself a cause of hypothalamic amenorrhoea (athlete triad).
C. Vitamins: correct micronutrient deficiencies but do not restore the energy and fat reserve needed to switch GnRH back on.
D. Sleep hygiene: useful for general wellbeing but has no role in reversing underweight-related amenorrhoea.
key_concept:
Underweight amenorrhoea: the fix is weight and fat gain.
  • Low body fat → low leptin → reduced GnRH pulses → low LH/FSH and oestrogen
  • Causes: undernutrition, eating disorders, excessive exercise, stress
  • Treatment: nutritional rehabilitation and weight restoration
  • Long-term risk if untreated: low bone density
  • Screen for an eating disorder in a very underweight adolescent
exam_pearl: In hypothalamic amenorrhoea, "exercise" is part of the cause, never the cure.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Also given as 'Q: 14 yo with lasting of her menarche, she is about to be less than 5th centile of her weight, which one of the following the highly contributing factor: A. Body fat (highlighted) B. Sleep hygiene C. Multivitamins'.

stem: What is the most common risk factor for abruptio placenta?
why_right: The question asks for the most common risk factor. Maternal hypertension (chronic hypertension or preeclampsia) is the most frequent association with placental abruption, ahead of smoking, cocaine use and abdominal trauma. Hypertensive vascular disease of the decidual vessels predisposes to retroplacental bleeding and separation.
why_wrong_block:
A. Folate deficiency: only a weak, historical association with abruption; its main obstetric link is neural tube defects and anaemia.
B. Short umbilical cord: a rare mechanical cause (traction on the placenta during descent), not a common one.
D. Premature rupture of membranes: a recognised risk factor (as is sudden uterine decompression), but much less common than hypertension.
key_concept:
Abruption risk factors: hypertension is the most common.
  • Hypertension or preeclampsia (most common)
  • Previous abruption
  • Smoking and cocaine
  • Abdominal trauma
  • Sudden decompression: PROM with polyhydramnios, delivery of first twin
exam_pearl: Painful bleeding with a tender, hard uterus is abruption; painless bleeding is previa.

stem: A pregnant woman has a history of preeclampsia in a previous pregnancy. What to do to prevent preeclampsia in the future pregnancy?
OptC: Restrict calcium intake to prevent hypertension
highlight_terms_source: history of preeclampsia in a previous pregnancy
why_right: A previous pregnancy with preeclampsia is a high-risk factor, and the only proven preventive measure is low-dose aspirin, started early in pregnancy (from about 12 weeks, before 16 weeks for most benefit) and continued until late pregnancy. It improves placentation and reduces the risk of recurrent and preterm preeclampsia.
why_wrong_block:
A. Complete bed rest: no proven benefit in preventing preeclampsia and increases the risk of venous thromboembolism.
C. Restrict calcium intake: the opposite of the evidence; calcium supplementation (not restriction) lowers preeclampsia risk in women with low dietary calcium intake.
D. Increase sodium intake: has no preventive effect and would not be advised in a woman at risk of hypertension.
key_concept:
Preeclampsia prevention in high-risk women: low-dose aspirin, started early.
  • High-risk: previous preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, CKD, autoimmune disease (SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome), multiple pregnancy
  • Aspirin: begin from about 12 weeks, ideally before 16 weeks
  • Calcium supplement if dietary intake is low
  • Not effective: bed rest, salt changes
exam_pearl: Aspirin prevents preeclampsia; magnesium sulfate prevents eclampsia (seizures) once preeclampsia is severe. Do not mix them up.

stem: Preterm rom was given a medication for prevention of respiratory distress. What is the medication?
why_right: The stem names the purpose of the drug: prevention of respiratory distress in a preterm baby after preterm ROM. Antenatal corticosteroids (betamethasone or dexamethasone) given before 34 weeks accelerate fetal lung maturation and surfactant production, cutting neonatal RDS, and also reduce intraventricular haemorrhage and necrotising enterocolitis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Ibuprofen: NSAIDs are not used here and risk premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus and oligohydramnios; indomethacin is the NSAID occasionally used as a tocolytic in early preterm labour.
C. Antibiotics: are indeed given in PPROM (e.g. ampicillin plus erythromycin) to prevent infection and prolong latency, but they do not prevent RDS.
D. Paracetamol: an analgesic and antipyretic only; no effect on fetal lung maturity.
key_concept:
PPROM drug bundle: each drug has its own job.
  • Steroids (before 34 weeks): fetal lungs, prevent RDS
  • Magnesium sulfate (before 32 weeks): fetal neuroprotection
  • Antibiotics: prevent infection, prolong latency
  • Tocolysis: avoid if chorioamnionitis is suspected
exam_pearl: If the stem names the goal (lungs, brain, infection), match the drug to that goal: lungs = steroids, brain = magnesium, infection = antibiotics.

stem: A 15-week pregnant woman who smokes regularly is worried that smoking might cause ADHD or other problems in her baby. What is the most appropriate management?
OptB: Refer her to a smoking cessation support group and counseling
OptC: Tell her to stop smoking abruptly without support
why_right: In pregnancy the first step for a smoker is behavioural support: structured counselling and referral to a cessation service, which is safe for the fetus and effective. Her worry about harm to the baby ("worried that smoking might cause ... problems") is a motivated moment to refer, not to lecture. Pharmacotherapy (NRT) is a second step in pregnancy, considered only if behavioural support alone fails.
why_wrong_block:
A. NRT is first line for non pregnant smokers, but in pregnancy it is added only after counselling alone has not worked; it still delivers nicotine to the fetus.
C. Telling her to stop abruptly with no support has the lowest success rate and abandons her; quitting should be encouraged, but always with structured support.
D. Option text missing in this recall. Another version listed non nicotine chewing gum, which is not an evidence based cessation therapy; bupropion and varenicline are generally avoided in pregnancy.
key_concept:
Smoking cessation in pregnancy: counselling/support first, drugs second.
  • Step 1: brief advice + referral to a cessation service/counselling
  • Step 2 (if fails): NRT, after discussing risks vs benefits
  • Bupropion, varenicline: generally avoided in pregnancy
  • Smoking risks: fetal growth restriction/low birth weight, preterm birth, abruption, stillbirth, SIDS
  • Non pregnant adult: NRT first line, varenicline next
exam_pearl: Do not carry over the general adult rule (NRT first) to a pregnant patient: in pregnancy support/counselling comes first.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Typed option D was 'Missing'. Embedded screenshot (file no. 291) version: options A. Prescribe NRT, B. Refer her to a smoking cessation program, C. Prescribe bupropion, D. Non-nicotine chewing gum; 'Right is: D. Non-nicotine chewing gum'.
Other marked answers: Screenshot 291: D. Non-nicotine chewing gum

stem: A 35-year-old woman diagnosed with left tubal ectopic pregnancy was treated with methotrexate. She remained asymptomatic with a plateauing of Beta hCG on day 4 and day 7. Which of the following is the most appropriate next management step?
OptB: Repeat Beta hCG in one week
highlight_terms_source: plateauing of Beta hCG on day 4 and day 7
key_concept:
After single dose MTX: compare day 4 vs day 7 beta hCG.
  • Fall >15%: weekly hCG until undetectable
  • Plateau or fall <15%: second dose of MTX
  • Rising: surgery (laparoscopy)
  • Rise from day 1 to day 4 is expected, not failure
  • Unstable/ruptured at any point: surgery
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Second dose of methotrexate.
exam_pearl: Plateau = repeat MTX; rise = surgery. Do not jump to salpingectomy in a stable patient whose hCG has only plateaued.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A pregnant female in her first trimester (10 wks I think) only values provided were normal Hb and normal hematocrit. Question was: How much iron does she need throughout her pregnancy?
highlight_terms_source: iron does she need throughout her pregnancy
why_right: The total extra iron needed across a singleton pregnancy is about 1000 mg. It covers iron transferred to the fetus and placenta, expansion of the maternal red cell mass, and ongoing basal losses. Her "normal Hb and hematocrit" do not change this: the requirement is physiological, which is why routine supplementation or dietary advice is given.
why_wrong_block:
B. 2000 mg is about double the accepted total requirement for a singleton pregnancy.
C. 3000 mg greatly overestimates the requirement; it exceeds the total body iron of most adult women.
D. 4000 mg is far above any physiological need and is not a quoted figure for pregnancy.
key_concept:
Iron requirement in pregnancy: about 1000 mg in total.
  • Goes to: fetus + placenta, maternal red cell mass expansion, basal losses
  • Demand rises mainly in the second and third trimesters
  • Plasma volume rises more than red cell mass, so Hb dilutes (physiological anemia)
  • Recommended daily intake in pregnancy: about 27 mg
exam_pearl: Total for the whole pregnancy is about 1 g; do not confuse it with the small daily intake figure.

stem: 32 year old females had never done HPV or pap smear. What should you do for primary prevention?
highlight_terms_source: never done HPV or pap smear
key_concept:
Levels of prevention applied to cervical cancer.
  • Primary: HPV vaccination, safer sex, smoking cessation
  • Secondary: Pap cytology / HPV testing to find precancer
  • Tertiary: treating established disease to limit harm
  • Screening: start at 21; 21 to 29 Pap every 3 years; 30 to 65 co test every 5 years or Pap every 3 years
exam_pearl: "Primary prevention" = vaccine; "screening" = Pap/HPV test. The lead in word decides, not her age.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: lady with previous ectopic pregnency, risk of developing an ectopic pregnancy in next pregnancy?
highlight_terms_source: risk of developing an ectopic pregnancy in next pregnancy
why_right: After one previous ectopic pregnancy, the risk of another ectopic in the next pregnancy is usually quoted as about 10 to 15%, and 15% is the option that sits in that band. Previous ectopic is the strongest single risk factor, because the underlying tubal damage often affects both tubes.
why_wrong_block:
A. 1 to 6% is close to the background population rate; it underestimates the recurrence risk after a previous ectopic.
B. 7 to 10% falls mostly below the quoted 10 to 15% band and only touches its lower edge; 15% is the better fit among these options.
D. 20% overestimates the risk after one ectopic; risks above 25% are quoted after two or more previous ectopics.
key_concept:
Ectopic recurrence risk.
  • One previous ectopic: about 10 to 15%
  • Two or more previous ectopics: >25%
  • Strongest individual risk factor: previous ectopic
  • Most common predisposing factor in the population: PID
  • Others: tubal/pelvic surgery, IVF, IUD in situ at conception, smoking
exam_pearl: Another version of this recall keys 10%; pick whichever option falls in the 10 to 15% band, and switch to >25% if she has had two or more ectopics.
compiler_note:
Compiler note: Second version (Q:): 'Pregnant concern she has history of ectopic pregnancy. Now she wants to know risk of ectopic pregnancy happen again? A. 1%, B. 5%, C. 10%, D. 15%' with 10% highlighted.
Other marked answers: Q restatement: 10%

stem: A 42-year-old P4+2 presented with severe, progressive secondary dysmenorrhea and menorrhagia. Pelvic examination demonstrated a tender, diffusely enlarged uterus (see report). Endometrial biopsy: Normal endometrium. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
why_right: A multiparous woman in her 40s (P4+2) with severe progressive secondary dysmenorrhea, menorrhagia and a tender, diffusely enlarged uterus is the classic picture of adenomyosis, where endometrial glands and stroma invade the myometrium. The normal endometrial biopsy is expected because the disease lies within the muscle wall, so a biopsy of the lining misses it.
why_wrong_block:
A. Endometritis: usually follows delivery, miscarriage or instrumentation with fever and discharge, and the biopsy would show inflammation (plasma cells); here the biopsy is normal.
B. Endometriosis: causes secondary dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and infertility but the uterus is usually normal in size; choose it when dysmenorrhea comes with infertility or an adnexal (chocolate) cyst.
D. Uterine sarcoma: a rapidly enlarging, often postmenopausal mass, not a long history of progressive painful heavy periods with a symmetric tender uterus.
key_concept:
Diffusely (symmetrically) enlarged, tender, boggy uterus + secondary dysmenorrhea + menorrhagia = adenomyosis.
  • Risk factors: multiparity, prior uterine surgery (e.g. myomectomy)
  • Endometrial biopsy is normal (disease is in the myometrium)
  • TVUS: myometrial thickening
  • Medical: hormonal IUD or OCP; definitive: hysterectomy
  • Fibroid: irregular firm enlargement; endometriosis: normal-sized uterus
exam_pearl: Symmetric uterus = adenomyosis; irregular lumpy uterus = fibroids; normal uterus with infertility = endometriosis.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Second version (Q:): 45-year-old P5+3 with AUB, regular cycle, clots and pain not relieved by analgesia, previous myomectomy and 3 surgical evacuations, bulky tender uterus, no adnexal mass, BMI 40. Options Adenomyosis / Endometriosis / Uterine fibroid / Endometrial cancer; Adenomyosis highlighted.

stem: A 20-year-old asymptomatic woman presented to the clinic with lower abdominal pain for 3 months (see lab result and report). Ultrasound: A multiloculated, solid, right adnexal complex mass of 6 cm. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
highlight_terms_source: multiloculated, solid, right adnexal complex mass of 6 cm
why_right: A 20-year-old with a 6 cm multiloculated, solid, complex adnexal mass has features that exclude observation (complex and larger than 5 cm). In a young woman the likely lesion is benign (often a germ cell tumor such as a dermoid), so surgical removal by ovary sparing cystectomy is preferred to preserve fertility and give histology.
why_wrong_block:
B. Oophorectomy removes the whole ovary unnecessarily in a 20-year-old; it fits a nonsalvageable ovary or postmenopausal women.
C. Review is only for simple, asymptomatic masses of 5 cm or less; this one is complex and 6 cm.
D. Aspiration of a complex or solid mass is non-diagnostic, recurs and risks spilling malignant cells; it has no role here.
key_concept:
Adnexal mass rule by features.
  • Simple, asymptomatic, 5 cm or less: reassess with ultrasound in 6 to 8 weeks
  • Complex, symptomatic, over 5 cm, or found at other surgery: cystectomy
  • Complex mass in postmenopausal woman or very high CA-125: gynecologic oncology
  • Young woman: ovary sparing surgery
exam_pearl: Same 6 cm complex mass at 76 years goes to gynecologic oncology; at 20 years it gets cystectomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: 'Answer: A' is printed after the second version (Q:): 21-year-old primigravida at 40 weeks, breech, planned CS; during surgery a right 5 cm ovarian cyst is observed; next step? A. Cystectomy, B. Oophorectomy, C. No intervention, D. Squeeze and rupture. Answer: A (Cystectomy).

stem: Pregnant women in 24 w of gestation on exam Baby is dead (Stillbirth case). Which of the following is best action
key_concept:
IUFD: confirm, investigate, deliver vaginally.
  • Confirm absent fetal heart activity on real time ultrasound
  • Check maternal clotting, signs of sepsis, pre eclampsia, abruption
  • Default: induction of labor (mifepristone then misoprostol)
  • Urgent delivery: sepsis, pre eclampsia, abruption, ruptured membranes, DIC
  • CS: only for maternal indications
  • Offer investigations for the cause and bereavement support
exam_pearl: A dead fetus is not an indication for cesarean; CS is reserved for maternal reasons.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: 20-years-old patient pregnant in 41 weeks of gestation. She wants spontaneous delivery to avoid bleeding. What to do for her?
OptA: Tell her Coming after 1 week for induction of labor
why_right: At 41 weeks induction would normally be offered, because stillbirth and placental insufficiency risks rise beyond term. Here she declines intervention and "wants spontaneous delivery", so the safe alternative is expectant management with increased fetal surveillance (regular CTG plus ultrasound for amniotic fluid), while continuing to offer induction.
why_wrong_block:
A. Sending her away for a week with no monitoring and planning induction only at 42 weeks leaves a late term fetus unsurveilled; if she wants to wait, monitoring must happen in the meantime.
B. Discharge without a plan ignores the rising risks after 41 weeks; it would be right only in a normal term pregnancy before 41 weeks.
D. Post term pregnancy alone is not an indication for cesarean; the route of delivery is induction of labor unless there is another obstetric indication.
key_concept:
Late term (41 weeks) and post term (42 weeks) pregnancy.
  • 41 weeks, accepts: induction of labor
  • 41 weeks, declines induction: increased fetal surveillance (CTG + amniotic fluid assessment)
  • Abnormal surveillance (e.g. decelerations, low fluid): deliver
  • 42 weeks: deliver; induction if no other indication for CS
exam_pearl: If the stem says she accepts management, the answer at 41 weeks is induction; surveillance is the answer only when she declines.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Original recall: 'Pregnant women 41 week gestation she indicate that she spontaneous delivery. Most appropriate action: A. cesarean section 42 week, B. induction of labor at 42 weeks, C. serial fetal surveillance' (unmarked).

stem: 55 years old woman presents with ASCUS positive. What is the next step in management?
key_concept:
ASC-US management by age.
  • 21 to 24: repeat Pap in 1 year
  • 25 or older: reflex HPV test
  • HPV positive: colposcopy
  • HPV negative: co test in 3 years
  • HPV not available: repeat Pap + HPV in 1 year
  • HSIL / ASC-H: colposcopy at any age
exam_pearl: ASC-US goes to HPV testing first; only ASC-H, HSIL or HPV positive ASC-US go straight to colposcopy.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 29-year-old woman with a history of primary hypothyroidism has been taking levothyroxine 100 mcg daily for the past three years. She comes to the clinic after a positive home pregnancy test. She feels well and has no new symptoms. Her most recent TSH level, checked two months ago, was within the normal range. She asks what she should do with her thyroid medication now that she is pregnant. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
OptA: Continue the same levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH in the third trimester
OptB: Increase the levothyroxine dose by approximately 25–30% and check TSH in 4–6 weeks
OptC: Stop levothyroxine temporarily and recheck thyroid function in one month
OptD: Switch from levothyroxine to liothyronine (T3) during pregnancy
why_right: Levothyroxine requirements rise early in pregnancy (higher thyroid binding globulin, larger volume of distribution, placental deiodination), and the fetus depends on maternal T4 in the first trimester. So a known hypothyroid woman should increase her dose by about 25 to 30% as soon as pregnancy is confirmed ("positive home pregnancy test"), even though she "feels well" with a normal TSH two months ago, then recheck TSH within 4 to 6 weeks.
why_wrong_block:
A. Keeping the same dose until the third trimester misses the early rise in requirement and risks maternal hypothyroidism during fetal brain development; TSH needs checking every few weeks in the first half of pregnancy.
C. Stopping levothyroxine is never appropriate in pregnancy; maternal hypothyroidism is linked to miscarriage and impaired fetal neurodevelopment.
D. Liothyronine (T3) does not cross the placenta well enough to supply fetal T4; levothyroxine remains the drug of choice in pregnancy.
key_concept:
Known hypothyroidism + new pregnancy: increase levothyroxine early.
  • Increase dose by about 25 to 30% at confirmation of pregnancy
  • Recheck TSH about every 4 weeks in the first half of pregnancy
  • Target: trimester specific TSH (lower than non pregnant)
  • Return to the pre pregnancy dose after delivery
exam_pearl: "Feels well with a normal TSH" is the trap: the increase is anticipatory, not driven by symptoms.

stem: Pregnant woman presents with a history of dyspnea, shortness of breath. Did Doppler US of both legs: normal. What is the best diagnostic test?
highlight_terms_source: Doppler US of both legs: normal
key_concept:
Suspected PE in pregnancy.
  • Step 1: bilateral compression ultrasound of the legs
  • DVT found: anticoagulate (no further imaging)
  • No DVT: V/Q scan (preferred with normal CXR) or CTPA
  • V/Q normal: stop; high probability: treat; non diagnostic: CTPA
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Ventilation-perfusion lung scan.
exam_pearl: Pregnant + negative leg Doppler + normal CXR = V/Q scan; non pregnant = CTPA.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Folic acid dose for pregnant lady with no risk factors?
why_right: The stem says "no risk factors", so she needs the low (average risk) dose of folic acid, not the high dose used for NTD risk states. The classic low dose is 0.4 mg daily, and guidance for average risk women allows 0.4 to 0.8 mg daily. Of the listed options, 0.8 mg is the only one inside that average risk range, so it is the recall's key.
why_wrong_block:
A. 0.2 mg is below the effective preventive dose for neural tube defects; no guideline uses it for pregnancy.
C. 1.4 mg is not a recognised regimen: too much for average risk and far short of the high dose (4 to 5 mg) used for high risk women.
D. 2.4 mg is also not a standard regimen; a high risk woman (previous NTD, antiepileptics, sickle cell disease, diabetes, obesity) would get 4 to 5 mg instead.
key_concept:
Folic acid dose depends on NTD risk.
  • Average risk: 0.4 mg daily (range 0.4 to 0.8 mg)
  • Start at least 1 month before conception, continue through the first trimester
  • High risk (previous NTD child, antiepileptics, diabetes, obesity): high dose 4 to 5 mg
  • Sickle cell disease / chronic hemolysis: 5 mg throughout pregnancy
exam_pearl: If 0.4 mg is listed, pick it; if not, the low dose answer is the one within 0.4 to 0.8 mg, never the 4 to 5 mg high dose.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Separate Q placed under 1238; 'Answer: B' printed at top of next page.

stem: A woman delivered a baby after 6 hours in labor with the umbilical cord around the neck. How can you prevent postpartum hemorrhage?
OptC: Cut and clamp the cord within 1–3 minutes
why_right: The question asks how to prevent PPH, which means active management of the third stage of labor. Its single most effective component is a uterotonic given right after delivery of the baby, and oxytocin 10 IU IM is the drug of choice. The cord around the neck is a distractor; it does not change PPH prophylaxis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Uterine massage is a treatment step once the uterus is found soft and boggy (atony); sustained massage is not recommended as prophylaxis when oxytocin has been given.
C. Delayed cord clamping (1 to 3 minutes) is recommended for neonatal benefit (iron stores), but it does not reduce maternal blood loss.
D. The recalled option is a cord manoeuvre (likely cord milking or traction); cord handling at most slightly affects maternal blood loss, while the uterotonic is the component that actually prevents PPH.
key_concept:
Active management of the third stage of labor prevents PPH.
  • Uterotonic after delivery of the baby: oxytocin 10 IU IM/IV (most important step)
  • Controlled cord traction: optional, minor benefit
  • Assess uterine tone after placenta delivery; massage if atonic
  • Treatment ladder for atony: oxytocin, then methylergonovine (avoid in hypertension), then carboprost (avoid in asthma)
exam_pearl: Prevention = oxytocin; uterine massage is what you do once bleeding from atony has started.

stem: A 26 years old lady, she is healthy, complaining of irritability and breast tenderness one week before menstrual cycle, she is asking for reducing her symptoms with exercises. Which type of exercises can be done?
highlight_terms_source: irritability and breast tenderness one week before
why_right: Irritability and breast tenderness one week before menses in a healthy woman is premenstrual syndrome. Lifestyle modification is step 1 of PMS treatment, and the exercise with the best support is regular aerobic exercise (brisk walking, cycling, swimming), which improves both mood and physical symptoms.
why_wrong_block: B. Flexibility and mobility work (stretching) is fine for general fitness but has little evidence for relieving PMS symptoms compared with aerobic activity.
key_concept:
PMS treatment ladder.
  • Step 1: lifestyle modification, especially regular aerobic exercise, sleep, reduce caffeine and salt
  • Step 2: SSRI (continuous or luteal phase only)
  • Step 3: combined OCP if contraception wanted or SSRI fails
  • Diagnosis is clinical: luteal symptoms that resolve within the first days of menses
exam_pearl: Exercise for PMS or dysmenorrhea on recalls is aerobic; drug therapy for severe PMS is an SSRI.

stem: A girl presents with symptoms of dysmenorrhea during her menstrual period. Which of the following types of exercise is recommended to help reduce the pain?
why_right: Painful menses in a young girl is primary dysmenorrhea. NSAIDs are the first line drug, and non drug measures (heat, regular exercise) are recommended alongside them. Regular aerobic exercise is the type recommended because it improves pelvic blood flow and releases endorphins, reducing menstrual pain.
why_wrong_block:
B. Flexibility and resistance training can help general fitness, but it is not the exercise type taught as recommended for dysmenorrhea.
C. Stability (core balance) exercise is used in rehabilitation and back pain programs, not as the standard advice for menstrual pain.
D. Agility training is sport specific skill work and has no role in managing dysmenorrhea.
key_concept:
Primary dysmenorrhea management.
  • Non drug measures: hot packs, regular aerobic exercise
  • NSAIDs: first line drug therapy
  • Combined OCP if NSAIDs fail or contraception is wanted
  • Secondary dysmenorrhea (older, worsening, pelvic pathology like endometriosis): investigate the cause
exam_pearl: Asked for exercise type: aerobic; asked for next step drug: NSAIDs.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot under 1253; answer printed in screenshot: A. Aerobic Exercise.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with amenorrhea for the past 6 weeks. What is the most appropriate initial test?
why_right: Any woman of reproductive age with amenorrhea must have pregnancy excluded first, because pregnancy is the most common cause. A urine or serum pregnancy test (beta hCG) is cheap, fast and decides the whole pathway, so it is the most appropriate initial test.
why_wrong_block:
A. TSH is part of the second tier workup of amenorrhea (thyroid disease), done only after a negative pregnancy test.
B. FSH separates ovarian failure from hypothalamic causes, but it is meaningful only once pregnancy has been ruled out.
D. Pelvic ultrasound comes after a positive test (to locate and date the pregnancy) or for structural causes; it is not the first test.
key_concept:
Amenorrhea workup order.
  • 1st: pregnancy test (beta hCG)
  • If negative: TSH, prolactin, FSH/LH
  • High FSH: ovarian insufficiency; low or normal FSH: hypothalamic/pituitary cause
  • High prolactin: look for drugs, hypothyroidism, then pituitary MRI
exam_pearl: Whatever the age or duration, reproductive age amenorrhea starts with a pregnancy test.

stem: The doctor ordered X-ray for patient, finds out later that she's pregnant in her first trimester. What should the doctor do?
OptD: Prioritize quality of images regardless of dose
why_right: When a woman is found to be pregnant after an X-ray, the first step is to establish the gestational age at the time of exposure. Fetal risk depends on timing (very early exposure tends to be all or none; organogenesis is the sensitive period) together with the estimated dose, so the doctor confirms gestational age (ideally by first trimester ultrasound crown rump length) before counselling. Most diagnostic X-rays give fetal doses far below those linked with harm, so termination is not indicated on that basis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Once pregnancy is known, imaging should not continue as for a non pregnant patient; it must be justified, use the lowest dose possible, or be replaced by ultrasound or MRI.
C. Indefinitely deferring needed imaging is wrong; it leaves the mother's condition undiagnosed, and the exposure that already happened is not undone by deferral.
D. Image quality regardless of dose breaks the ALARA principle (as low as reasonably achievable), which matters most in pregnancy.
key_concept:
Radiation exposure discovered in early pregnancy.
  • Confirm gestational age at exposure (CRL on first trimester ultrasound)
  • Estimate fetal dose (medical physicist if needed)
  • Counsel: routine diagnostic X-ray doses are far below the threshold for fetal harm
  • Future imaging: justify, ALARA, prefer ultrasound or MRI
exam_pearl: Accidental X-ray in pregnancy is never by itself an indication for termination; date the pregnancy and counsel.

stem: A 24-year-old primigravida at her 11th week of pregnancy presents with lethargy, constipation, and intolerance to cold temperature. Laboratory investigations reveal an elevated TSH level. The mother is anxious about her baby and fears intellectual disability. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Lethargy, constipation and cold intolerance with an elevated TSH at 11 weeks is overt hypothyroidism in pregnancy. Treatment is levothyroxine (thyroxine), started promptly, because the fetus depends on maternal thyroid hormone in the first trimester and untreated hypothyroidism is linked to impaired neurodevelopment, which is exactly the mother's fear.
why_wrong_block:
A. Propylthiouracil is an antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism (the first trimester choice in Graves disease); it would worsen hypothyroidism.
B. Multivitamins do not replace thyroid hormone and will not correct the deficiency.
D. Thyroidectomy is for hyperthyroidism or goitre not controlled medically; it would cause, not treat, hypothyroidism.
key_concept:
Thyroid disease in pregnancy.
  • High TSH + symptoms: levothyroxine
  • Requirement rises in pregnancy; known hypothyroid women increase the dose when pregnant
  • Hyperthyroid first trimester: PTU; later: methimazole
  • Radioactive iodine: contraindicated in pregnancy
exam_pearl: High TSH = hypothyroid = thyroxine; PTU is the trap option for the opposite disease.

stem: 17YO female has amenorrhea for 6 weeks, comes with mild bleeding. Cervical os is open, also there's bleeding and pain. What is next?
why_right: Six weeks of amenorrhea with bleeding, pain and an open cervical os means an inevitable or incomplete miscarriage. After history and pelvic examination, the next step is transvaginal ultrasound, which confirms an intrauterine pregnancy, checks for retained products and viability, and excludes ectopic pregnancy, so treatment can be chosen by type.
why_wrong_block:
A. Pelvic MRI has no role in first trimester bleeding; it is slow and costly and adds nothing over TVUS.
C. Serial beta hCG at 48 hours is for a pregnancy of unknown location after a nondiagnostic TVUS, not the first step with an open os.
D. Waiting 10 days is unsafe; an open os with bleeding is an ongoing miscarriage that needs assessment now.
key_concept:
Early pregnancy bleeding: history and exam, then TVUS, then treat by type.
  • Closed os + viable fetus: threatened
  • Open os, no tissue passed: inevitable
  • Open os, some tissue passed: incomplete
  • Closed os, all tissue passed, empty uterus: complete
  • Closed os, nonviable, nothing passed: missed
exam_pearl: Bleeding plus open os: TVUS next; serial hCG only when TVUS cannot locate the pregnancy.

stem: 31YO female trying to conceive for 3 years but unsuccessful, semen analysis normal, BMI 32, wants IVF.
why_right: She has infertility with a normal semen analysis and BMI 32, with no tubal factor shown. Obesity impairs ovulation and lowers success of every fertility treatment, so the first step is weight loss (lifestyle modification) followed by ovulation induction. IVF is reserved for specific indications or failure of simpler treatment, not chosen first because the patient requests it.
why_wrong_block: A. IVF first is right for bilateral tubal blockage, severe male factor or failed ovulation induction; none is present here, and obesity should be addressed first.
key_concept:
Infertility approach.
  • Semen analysis first; if normal, assess the female
  • Ovulation: cycle history, FSH, LH, prolactin, mid luteal progesterone
  • Tubes: HSG; bilateral block confirmed: IVF
  • Anovulation / PCOS: weight loss first, then ovulation induction (clomiphene)
  • IVF after failed induction or for tubal / severe male factor
exam_pearl: Obese anovulatory woman wanting IVF: lifestyle and induction first; only blocked tubes jump straight to IVF.

stem: Women last period was 6 weeks she came with mild vaginl bleeding without abdomen pain us no intrauterine gestational sac labs bhcg first 3000. Seconds 7000 third week 16000?
why_right: The first scan showed no intrauterine sac, so serial beta hCG has already been done: 3000, 7000, 16000, steadily rising, a pattern typical of a growing pregnancy. The hCG is now well above the discriminatory zone, so a gestational sac should be visible; the next step is to repeat the pelvic (transvaginal) ultrasound to locate the pregnancy. An intrauterine sac confirms an intrauterine pregnancy; an empty uterus at this level makes ectopic pregnancy very likely.
why_wrong_block:
A. Methotrexate is never given before an ectopic is confirmed (it could end a viable intrauterine pregnancy), and an hCG of 16000 is above the level where methotrexate is suitable.
B. Repeating hCG at 48 hours is the step for a pregnancy of unknown location while hCG is still low; here the rising trend is already known and well above the discriminatory zone, so another hCG adds nothing.
D. Reassurance is unsafe until the pregnancy is seen inside the uterus; ectopic has not been excluded.
key_concept:
Pregnancy of unknown location (positive test, no sac on TVUS).
  • Step 1: repeat beta hCG in 48 hours
  • Viable IUP: usually near doubling; a 48 hour rise below about 35% is abnormal
  • Slow rise, plateau or fall: ectopic or failing pregnancy
  • hCG above the discriminatory zone (classically 1500 to 2000, some use up to 3500): repeat TVUS, a sac should be seen
  • No IUP above the discriminatory zone: ectopic until proven otherwise
exam_pearl: First empty scan: repeat hCG; once hCG passes the discriminatory zone: repeat the ultrasound.

stem: 4 years old primigravida qin 37 week presented with blood pressure 160/100 mmhg and she was irritable, fundus hight was 35 cm and cervix was soft, 1 cm dilated, with intact membrane fetus was 2.2 kg and low amniotic fluid. Doppler show absent umbilical artery Whats the appropriate management?
why_right: BP 160/100 with irritability at 37 weeks is pre-eclampsia with severe features at term, so delivery is required now. The decisive extra clue is the absent umbilical artery end-diastolic flow in a small fetus (2.2 kg) with low fluid: this is a compromised, placentally insufficient fetus that is unlikely to tolerate contractions. With an unfavourable cervix (only 1 cm) a long induction would add risk, so caesarean section is the delivery route this card keys.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amniotomy is only one step of induction, used when the cervix is already favourable and the head engaged; here the cervix is 1 cm, fluid is low and the fetus is compromised.
C. Induction is the right answer for the same term pre-eclamptic with a reassuring fetus (the sister card without the Doppler finding); absent end-diastolic flow makes a trial of labour unsafe.
D. Waiting has no role at term in pre-eclampsia with severe-range BP; delivery is the cure and delay risks eclampsia, HELLP, abruption and fetal death.
key_concept:
Term pre-eclampsia means deliver; the fetal Doppler decides the route.
  • Pre-eclampsia at ≥37 weeks: deliver
  • Reassuring fetus + soft cervix: induction of labour
  • UA absent end-diastolic flow at ≥34 weeks: deliver
  • UA reversed end-diastolic flow at ≥32 weeks: deliver
  • AEDV/REDV + unripe cervix: caesarean favoured
  • Amniotomy: only with a favourable cervix
exam_pearl: Same stem twice: with absent end-diastolic flow the answer is CS; without it the answer is induction.
compiler_note: ⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-1293 → C. induction of labor. Confirm before the exam.

stem: 4 years old primigravida qin 37 week presented with blood pressure 160/100 mmhg and she was irritable, fundus hight was 35 cm and cervix was soft, 1 cm dilated, with intact membrane fetus was 2.2 kg and low amniotic fluid. Whats the appropriate management?
why_right: BP 160/100 with irritability at 37 weeks is pre-eclampsia with severe features at term, so the pregnancy should be delivered. This version gives no Doppler abnormality, and the cervix is soft and 1 cm, so a vaginal route is reasonable: induction of labour (with cervical ripening first if the Bishop score is low), alongside BP control and magnesium sulfate. Caesarean is reserved for a separate obstetric indication.
why_wrong_block:
A. Amniotomy is one method within induction, suitable once the cervix is favourable and the head engaged; at 1 cm with low fluid, ripening and oxytocin come first, so 'induction' is the better overall answer.
B. Pre-eclampsia alone is not an indication for caesarean; CS is chosen when there is fetal compromise (e.g. absent end-diastolic flow, as in the sister card), non-reassuring CTG or malpresentation.
D. Expectant care is wrong at term with severe-range BP; delivery is the only cure and waiting risks eclampsia, HELLP and abruption.
key_concept:
Pre-eclampsia at term: deliver, vaginally unless there is an obstetric reason not to.
  • ≥37 weeks: induction of labour
  • Severe features: stabilise BP + MgSO4, then deliver
  • Unfavourable cervix (low Bishop score): ripen with vaginal prostaglandin before oxytocin
  • Favourable cervix (Bishop ≥8): amniotomy + oxytocin
  • Fetal compromise (AEDV/REDV, bad CTG): caesarean
exam_pearl: The only difference from the CS version of this question is the absent umbilical artery flow; no Doppler problem means induction.
compiler_note:
⚠ The same question appears elsewhere in this file with a DIFFERENT marked answer: AS-1292 → B. CS. Confirm before the exam.
Compiler note: Same scenario as 1292 but without the absent umbilical artery Doppler finding.

stem: Women with dysmenorrhea (what is the important in her history ?
why_right: For a woman with dysmenorrhea, the menstrual history carries the diagnosis: age at onset relative to menarche, timing of pain within the cycle, duration, cycle regularity, flow and associated symptoms. These separate primary dysmenorrhea (starts within 1 to 2 years of menarche, no pelvic pathology) from secondary causes such as endometriosis, adenomyosis or fibroids.
why_wrong_block:
A. Family history (e.g. endometriosis in a mother or sister) is supportive only; it does not characterise her pain.
B. Medical history matters for drug choice (e.g. NSAID contraindications) but does not distinguish primary from secondary dysmenorrhea.
C. Surgical history helps when adhesions or previous pelvic surgery are suspected, but it is secondary to the menstrual pattern itself.
key_concept:
Dysmenorrhea work-up starts with the menstrual history.
  • Primary: onset within 1 to 2 years of menarche, normal pelvis
  • Secondary: later onset, underlying pathology
  • Endometriosis: dysmenorrhea + dyspareunia + infertility
  • Adenomyosis: dysmenorrhea + menorrhagia + bulky boggy uterus
  • Primary: NSAIDs first, then combined pill
exam_pearl: Any 'most important history' question about a menstrual symptom points to the menstrual history.

stem: Pregnant lady came in booked clinic ask how to provide best care for her self and the child ?
OptA: nutrition rich in iron and folic acid.
highlight_terms_source: how to provide best care for her self and the child
why_right: At the booking visit she asks what will give the best care for herself and the baby. Of the options, only a diet rich in iron and folic acid is a positive, evidence-based measure: folic acid lowers neural tube defect risk, and iron meets the rising demand of pregnancy and prevents iron deficiency anaemia, the commonest anaemia in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Delaying care is the opposite of advice; booking should be in the first trimester (dating scan, screening bloods), with visits every 4 weeks until 28 weeks, every 2 weeks until 36, then weekly.
C. Healthy pregnant women are encouraged to stay active with regular moderate exercise; avoiding activity offers no benefit and promotes excess weight gain.
D. This option was not recorded by the recaller, so it cannot be judged; the key remains nutrition with iron and folic acid.
key_concept:
Antenatal advice: book early, eat well, supplement, stay active.
  • Folic acid 0.4 mg daily (high risk of NTD: high dose)
  • Iron rich diet; iron supplement if anaemic
  • Booking visit in first trimester
  • Visits: 4 weekly to 28, 2 weekly to 36, then weekly
  • Regular moderate exercise is encouraged
exam_pearl: Options that delay care or restrict normal activity are almost never the 'best care' answer in pregnancy.

stem: Female with an asymptomatic 2 cm subserosal fibroid. And is afraid it might affect her future pregnancy. What will you advise her ?
why_right: An asymptomatic, small (2 cm), subserosal fibroid needs no treatment, only reassurance and periodic ultrasound follow up. Subserosal fibroids project outward from the uterus and do not distort the cavity, so they have little or no effect on conception or pregnancy; submucosal fibroids are the type linked to infertility and miscarriage.
why_wrong_block:
B. There is no reason to avoid pregnancy; most small fibroids cause no problem, and avoiding pregnancy would be harmful advice.
C. Myomectomy is for symptomatic or large fibroids, failed medical treatment, or a cavity-distorting (submucosal) fibroid causing infertility; operating on a 2 cm subserosal fibroid adds uterine scarring with no benefit.
D. Hysterectomy ends fertility and is for symptomatic women who have completed their family; it is clearly wrong for a woman planning pregnancy.
key_concept:
Fibroid management is driven by symptoms, size and location.
  • Asymptomatic, incidental: reassure + annual ultrasound
  • Submucosal: bleeding, infertility, miscarriage; hysteroscopic resection
  • Subserosal: pressure symptoms, rarely bleeding or infertility
  • Medical: OCP; GnRH analogue to shrink before surgery
  • Surgery: large (>7 cm) or failed medical treatment
  • Fertility wanted: myomectomy, not hysterectomy
exam_pearl: If the fibroid were submucosal and she had infertility, the answer would flip to hysteroscopic myomectomy.

stem: 35 years old P2 pregnant lady She had previous pregnancy with IUGR with weight 1.6kg after delivery at 34 weeks ,She concerned about current pregnancy (20 weeks gestation) What is most appropriate action at this pregnancy ?
OptD: Doppler blood flow of umbilical cord
why_right: A previous IUGR baby (1.6 kg at 34 weeks) makes this pregnancy high risk for recurrent growth restriction. At 20 weeks with no current problem, the most appropriate plan is serial ultrasound for fetal growth (estimated fetal weight, abdominal circumference, liquor) through the third trimester, which detects FGR early; Doppler and fetal wellbeing tests are then added if growth falls off.
why_wrong_block:
A. CTG assesses fetal wellbeing in the third trimester or in labour; it does not measure growth and has no role at 20 weeks.
