B. BPP is a wellbeing test used once FGR is established or in late pregnancy surveillance; it does not screen for growth restriction.
D. Umbilical artery Doppler is the key monitoring test once a small fetus is found (absent or reversed flow guides delivery timing), but it is not the primary screening tool in a currently normal pregnancy.
key_concept:
Previous FGR: screen growth with serial scans, then monitor a small fetus with Doppler.
  • Fundal height lags or high risk history: serial ultrasound growth
  • FGR confirmed: weekly UA Doppler + BPP + NST
  • UA absent end-diastolic flow ≥34 weeks: deliver
  • UA reversed end-diastolic flow ≥32 weeks: deliver
  • Reassuring tests: deliver at ≥37 weeks
exam_pearl: Growth problem not yet present means serial growth scans; small fetus already found means umbilical artery Doppler.

stem: 30 year old 37 week primigravida came after spontaneous rupture of membrane, delivered after 5h SVD with 2nd degree perianal tear, placenta was not delivered, they have to remove it manually. Prophylaxis antibiotics given for what?
OptB: Rupture of membrane more than 6 hours before delivery
highlight_terms_source: placenta was not delivered, they have to remove it manually
why_right: Of the events listed, manual removal of the placenta is the recognised indication for prophylactic antibiotics: the operator's hand passes through the cervix into the uterine cavity, carrying a real risk of endometritis, so a single prophylactic dose is recommended. The other events (normal delivery, a 2nd degree tear, membranes ruptured about 5 hours) do not need antibiotics.
why_wrong_block:
A. A spontaneous vaginal delivery by itself is not an indication for antibiotic prophylaxis.
B. Membranes ruptured only about 5 hours before delivery is not prolonged rupture; prolonged rupture (classically ≥18 hours) is what raises infection and GBS concern.
C. A 2nd degree tear (perineal muscle, sphincter intact) is repaired without antibiotics; prophylaxis is given for 3rd and 4th degree (anal sphincter or rectal mucosa) tears.
key_concept:
Antibiotic prophylaxis around delivery: instrumentation of the uterus or sphincter injury.
  • Manual removal of placenta: prophylactic antibiotics
  • Caesarean section: prophylactic antibiotics
  • 3rd or 4th degree tear: antibiotics
  • 1st or 2nd degree tear: none
  • Retained placenta: wait 30 min, then manual removal; D&C only if removal fails or tissue is retained
exam_pearl: A 2nd degree tear tempts students, but only 3rd and 4th degree tears earn antibiotics.

stem: A 30-year-old primigravida at 6 weeks of gestation presenting to the Emergency Room with mild abdominal pains. On examination, the abdomen is soft, non-tender. The pelvic examination reveals a normal cervix with mild cervical motion tenderness. The patient lives 80 km away from the hospital and her husband is participating in a mission in a different city. She was brought to the Emergency Room by her neighbour (see lab results and report). Blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, Heart rate 76/min, Respiratory rate 18/min, Temperature 36.6 °C. Hb 110 (130-170 g/L male, 120-160 g/L female). hCG 5000 (< 5). Trans-vaginal ultrasound: normal sized uterus with no clear gestational sac and a 4 cm right adnexal mass with no fetal pole. Which of the patient characteristics favour surgical management?
highlight_terms_source: lives 80 km away from the hospital
husband is participating in a mission in a different city
no clear gestational sac and a 4 cm right adnexal mass
why_right: She is hemodynamically stable (BP 110/70, HR 76) with an unruptured ectopic, so methotrexate could otherwise be considered. Methotrexate, however, demands a compliant patient who can return for serial hCG on set days and reach hospital fast if the tube ruptures. She lives 80 km away, her husband is in another city and a neighbour brought her: the social history makes reliable follow up unsafe, which favours surgery.
why_wrong_block:
A. Her vital signs are normal; instability would favour surgery (as an absolute contraindication to methotrexate), but here they argue for, not against, medical treatment.
B. hCG 5000 still meets the methotrexate criterion (≤5000), so it does not push her to surgery; only a level above the cutoff would make hCG the deciding factor.
D. A 4 cm mass without fetal cardiac activity is at the size limit and is a relative factor; a larger mass, fetal heartbeat or free fluid would make ultrasound the deciding feature.
key_concept:
Methotrexate needs ALL of the criteria; failing any one pushes to surgery.
  • Hemodynamically stable, unruptured
  • hCG ≤5000
  • No fetal cardiac activity
  • Mass <4 cm
  • Compliant, able to attend serial hCG follow up
  • Unstable or ruptured: surgery after resuscitation
exam_pearl: When the stem goes out of its way to describe distance and absent support, the answer is social history.

stem: Previous past expulsion at 22 wks. Painless expulsion (no mention of cervical dilatation). Now 10 wks. What to do?
why_right: A previous painless expulsion at 22 weeks is a second trimester loss typical of cervical incompetence. With that history the woman is offered a history-indicated (prophylactic) cerclage at about 12 to 14 weeks, after the first trimester miscarriage window and once a viable, normal pregnancy is confirmed. She is now 10 weeks, so the plan is cerclage at 13 weeks.
why_wrong_block: B. 18 weeks is too late for a history-indicated stitch; from 15 to 23 weeks the approach is serial transvaginal cervical length, and cerclage is placed only if the cervix shortens below 25 mm (ultrasound-indicated) before 24 weeks.
key_concept:
Cervical incompetence: previous mid-trimester painless loss decides the plan.
  • Previous 2nd trimester loss, now early: cerclage at 12 to 14 weeks
  • Previous loss, now 15 to 23 weeks: serial cervical length; cerclage if <25 mm
  • No previous loss, short cervix at 20 weeks: vaginal progesterone
  • Cerclage not generally done after 24 weeks
exam_pearl: History alone gives cerclage at 13 weeks; a short cervix on scan gives cerclage later.
compiler_note: Compiler note: History-indicated cerclage: 12-14 weeks. Ultrasound-indicated cerclage: when cervical length <25 mm before 24 weeks.

stem: Postcoital bleeding irregular cycle no abdominal masses, next?
why_right: Postcoital bleeding is a cervical symptom until proven otherwise: cervical dysplasia, cervical cancer, ectropion, polyps or cervicitis bleed on contact. With a normal abdomen (no pelvic mass), the next step is to assess the cervix with a speculum examination and a Pap smear. The 'irregular cycle' is a distractor that tempts you toward the uterus.
why_wrong_block: B. Vaginal ultrasound images the endometrium and adnexa; it would be the right first test for suspected uterine or adnexal pathology (e.g. a pelvic mass or AUB workup), but it cannot exclude a cervical lesion causing contact bleeding.
key_concept:
Postcoital bleeding = think cervix first.
  • No visible lesion: Pap smear (cervical cytology)
  • Visible cervical lesion or mass: colposcopy directed biopsy (punch biopsy), not Pap
  • Pap shows HSIL, ASC-H or cancer: colposcopy plus biopsy
  • Uterine causes (AUB, endometrial pathology): TVUS / endometrial sampling
exam_pearl: If the stem mentions a visible cervical mass, the answer flips from Pap smear to directed biopsy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Postcoital bleeding is a red flag for cervical pathology, especially cervical cancer or cervical dysplasia. The first step in evaluation is screening the cervix with a Papanicolaou test.

stem: Pregnant lady in the last trimester Dx with peripartum cardiomyopathy what to give
why_right: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is systolic heart failure presenting late in pregnancy or in the months after delivery, so it is treated like HFrEF but with pregnancy-safe drugs. While she is still pregnant ("last trimester"), ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated, so afterload is reduced with hydralazine (usually combined with nitrates), alongside beta-blockers and loop diuretics for congestion.
why_wrong_block:
A. Losartan is an ARB; ARBs are fetotoxic (fetal renal damage, oligohydramnios) and contraindicated in pregnancy. They become an option for HF only after delivery.
B. Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor, contraindicated in pregnancy for the same fetal renal effects; after delivery an ACE inhibitor replaces hydralazine/nitrates for PPCM.
D. Methyldopa is an antihypertensive for chronic or gestational hypertension; it has no role in reducing afterload or improving outcomes in heart failure.
key_concept:
PPCM drug choice depends on whether she is still pregnant.
  • Antepartum: hydralazine + nitrates (afterload), beta-blocker, loop diuretic if congested
  • Postpartum: switch to ACE inhibitor/ARB (avoid some if breastfeeding per drug)
  • ACEi/ARB in pregnancy: contraindicated (fetal renal toxicity)
  • Methyldopa / labetalol: hypertension in pregnancy, not HF therapy
exam_pearl: Same disease, different answer: pregnant = hydralazine/nitrates; postpartum = ACE inhibitor.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is systolic HF in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months postpartum; treat as HF using pregnancy-safe drugs: diuretics (furosemide), beta-blockers, vasodilators like hydralazine, nitrates. ACEI/ARBs are teratogenic (losartan ARB, lisinopril ACEI contraindicated). Hydralazine is a safe vasodilator in pregnancy and reduces afterload. Methyldopa is used for gestational hypertension, not HF. In HF including PPCM: avoid ACEI/ARB, use hydralazine + nitrates.

stem: A woman presents with vaginal dryness, fatigue, excessive sweating, and secondary amenorrhea. What is the first test should perform?
why_right: The symptoms (vaginal dryness, sweating, fatigue) point toward estrogen deficiency such as menopause or premature ovarian insufficiency, but the lead-in asks for the first test in secondary amenorrhea. Pregnancy is the most common cause of secondary amenorrhea in any woman of reproductive age, so a pregnancy test always comes first before any hormonal workup.
why_wrong_block:
A. FSH confirms menopause or POI and would be the key test once pregnancy is excluded; it is the second step here, not the first.
B. Thyroid tests (TSH) are part of the second tier of amenorrhea workup (with prolactin) after a negative pregnancy test; thyroid disease can mimic fatigue and sweating but is not checked first.
D. Estradiol level is not a reliable first-line test; it fluctuates and adds little once FSH is measured, and it does not exclude pregnancy.
key_concept:
Secondary amenorrhea: rule out pregnancy first, every time.
  • Step 1: beta-hCG
  • Step 2 (not pregnant): TSH, prolactin, FSH
  • High FSH + vasomotor symptoms: menopause (≥45), early menopause (40 to 45), POI (before 40)
  • Other causes: PCOS, hypothyroidism, hypothalamic causes (stress, weight loss, exercise), hyperprolactinemia, drugs
exam_pearl: Menopausal-sounding symptoms tempt you to pick FSH, but 'first test' in amenorrhea is always the pregnancy test.

stem: Management of asymptomatic tubal ectopic pregnancy
key_concept:
Tubal ectopic management fork:
  • Unstable / ruptured: surgery (laparoscopy preferred, laparotomy if shocked)
  • Stable + hCG ≤5000, mass <4 cm, no heartbeat, compliant: methotrexate
  • Mass ≥4 cm or cardiac activity: surgery
  • Asymptomatic + low, declining hCG: expectant
  • After MTX: rising hCG day 4 to 7 means surgery
exam_pearl: 'Asymptomatic' is the trap: look for the hCG trend and size; a low falling hCG favors expectant, criteria-met favors methotrexate.

stem: Pregnant at 37 weeks of gestation undergoes an ultrasound that reveals a fundal height corresponding to 35 weeks, US shows absent end-diastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler. What is the appropriate next step in management?
key_concept:
Umbilical artery Doppler in FGR:
  • Normal/reassuring: weekly UA Doppler, BPP, NST; deliver at ≥37 weeks
  • AEDV: deliver at ≥34 weeks; below that, daily testing and steroids
  • REDV: deliver at ≥32 weeks; below that, daily testing and steroids
  • Absent or reversed EDF: many guidelines favor caesarean delivery
exam_pearl: Once EDF is absent or reversed past the cut-off gestation, 'repeat scan later' is never right; the debate is only induction versus caesarean.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: Female patient with ectopic pregnancy with first hCG reading of 3000, after that 3100, after that 2900. Which of the following recommended management
why_right: After single-dose methotrexate, beta-hCG is compared between day 4 (3100) and day 7 (2900). That is a fall of only about 6 to 7%, less than the required 15%, which means an inadequate response. With hCG not rising and no sign of rupture, the recommended step is a second dose of methotrexate.
why_wrong_block:
A. Surgery is for a rising hCG between day 4 and day 7, rupture, hemodynamic instability or failure after a second dose; none is present here.
C. Observation alone is correct only when hCG falls by more than 15% from day 4 to day 7; then weekly hCG until undetectable.
key_concept:
Methotrexate follow-up: compare day 4 with day 7.
  • Fall >15%: weekly hCG until undetectable
  • Plateau or fall <15%: second methotrexate dose
  • Rising hCG or rupture signs: surgery
  • A rise from day 1 to day 4 is expected and not failure
exam_pearl: Do not compare day 0 to day 7; the 3000 baseline is a distractor, the decision uses day 4 versus day 7.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Screenshot 0589 (next page): 26-year-old treated with methotrexate for ectopic; BhCG baseline 3000 on injection day, day 4 3100, day 7 2900. Options: A. Immediate laparotomy B. Reassure and continue monitoring C. Multiple dose regimen of methotrexate D. Counsel for the possibility of administering a second methotrexate dose. Answer: D (consistent with typed highlight).

stem: (Fragment under 1435, stem not recalled) There Was No Diabetes , Nor Obesity
OptA: She is at significant risk of endometrial cancer
OptB: She is at increased risk for multiple gestation
OptC: She is at increased risk of ovarian cancer
OptD: She is at significant risk of osteoporosis
why_right: The stem was not recalled, but this option set belongs to the classic premature ovarian insufficiency question: a young woman with secondary amenorrhea, very high FSH and LH, negative pregnancy test. POI is a low-estrogen state, and loss of estrogen accelerates bone resorption, so the main long-term risk is osteoporosis. The recalled clue 'no diabetes nor obesity' removes the usual endometrial cancer risk factors.
why_wrong_block:
A. Endometrial cancer comes from unopposed estrogen (obesity, PCOS, diabetes, anovulation); POI is hypoestrogenic, and the stem stresses no diabetes or obesity.
B. Multiple gestation is a risk of ovulation induction or IVF; in ovarian failure fertility is markedly reduced.
C. Ovarian cancer risk rises with incessant ovulation (nulliparity, BRCA); a failed ovary that no longer ovulates does not raise it.
key_concept:
POI: menopause before 40.
  • Labs: high FSH and LH, low estrogen, negative hCG
  • Risks: osteoporosis, cardiovascular disease, infertility, vasomotor and vaginal symptoms
  • Treatment: HRT until the usual age of menopause (bone and symptom protection)
  • Contrast: PCOS/obesity = unopposed estrogen = endometrial cancer
exam_pearl: High FSH means low estrogen: think bone loss, not endometrial cancer, which belongs to high-estrogen states.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Orphan option set printed under 1435 without its own stem; D highlighted.

stem: A 29-year-old G4 P3003 at 12 weeks' gestation. Her current pregnancy has been uneventful. One week ago she has noticed swelling of her ankles and feet (see lab results). Blood pressure 150/95 mmHg, Heart rate 84 /minute, Temperature 36.9°C, Respiratory Rate 15 /minute. Test / Result / Normal Values: Hb 11.9 (120-158 g/L); Creatinine 65 (58-145 pmol/L); Uric acid 210 (140-360 pmol/L); Urine analysis Trace protein. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy?
why_right: Hypertension (150/95) at 12 weeks, before 20 weeks, is chronic (pre-existing) hypertension, not pre-eclampsia; normal creatinine and uric acid with only trace protein support this. It needs a pregnancy-safe oral agent: labetalol is first line and methyldopa is the safe alternative, and it is the only safe drug listed.
why_wrong_block:
B. Atenolol is avoided in pregnancy because it is associated with fetal growth restriction; the beta-blocker of choice is labetalol.
C. Captopril is an ACE inhibitor; ACE inhibitors are fetotoxic (renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios) and contraindicated in pregnancy.
D. Losartan is an ARB, contraindicated in pregnancy for the same fetal renal toxicity as ACE inhibitors.
key_concept:
Hypertension in pregnancy: timing gives the diagnosis.
  • Before 20 weeks: chronic hypertension
  • After 20 weeks, no proteinuria: gestational hypertension
  • After 20 weeks + proteinuria or end-organ signs: pre-eclampsia
  • Oral: labetalol first, methyldopa second, nifedipine alternative
  • IV acute severe: labetalol, hydralazine
  • Never: ACE inhibitors, ARBs; avoid atenolol
exam_pearl: Ankle swelling and trace protein tempt pre-eclampsia, but at 12 weeks it is chronic hypertension; the drug choice is the same safe list.

stem: Female after 24 h of rupture of membrane she get SV birth What is best PREVENTION for pelvic infection
key_concept:
Postpartum endometritis is polymicrobial; prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, cesarean and many vaginal examinations raise the risk.
  • Treatment of endometritis: IV clindamycin + gentamicin until afebrile
  • Chorioamnionitis in labor: IV ampicillin + gentamicin, then deliver
  • Unknown GBS status with rupture of membranes for 18 hours or more at term: intrapartum GBS prophylaxis (penicillin or ampicillin)
  • Routine antibiotics are not needed after an uncomplicated vaginal birth
exam_pearl: Clindamycin is the anaerobic arm and gentamicin the gram negative arm; vancomycin alone covers neither.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 59-year-old woman undergoes a hysteroscopy secondary to her complain of abnormal uterine bleeding for the last couple of months (see image). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Same as Joes recalls US pic
key_concept:
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to Endometrial polyps.
  • Hysteroscopy sees only the cavity: polyps and submucosal fibroids
  • Polyp: soft, smooth, vascular, pedunculated
  • Submucosal fibroid: firm, pale, broad based
  • Adenomyosis: myometrium (ultrasound/MRI)
  • Endometriosis and subserosal fibroid: outside the cavity (laparoscopy)
  • Postmenopausal polyp with bleeding: hysteroscopic removal and histology
exam_pearl: Ask where the lesion lives: inside the cavity, in the wall, or outside the uterus; only cavity lesions appear on hysteroscopy.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A pregnant woman presents with an enlarged goiter. Laboratory tests show elevated TSH. She is concerned about her baby's intelligence. What is the most appropriate management?
why_right: A goiter with elevated TSH in pregnancy means hypothyroidism, and untreated maternal hypothyroidism is linked to impaired fetal neurodevelopment, which is exactly her concern about the baby's intelligence. The treatment is levothyroxine (thyroxine), which is safe in pregnancy and restores normal maternal hormone levels for the fetal brain. The dose is titrated to trimester specific TSH targets.
why_wrong_block:
B. Carbimazole is an antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism (low TSH) and would worsen hypothyroidism; it is also avoided in the first trimester because of embryopathy, where PTU is preferred.
C. Iodine supplementation prevents deficiency in at risk populations but does not treat established hypothyroidism with a raised TSH; radioactive iodine is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
D. Surgery is for a compressive goiter, suspected malignancy or hyperthyroidism failing drugs; it does not correct hypothyroidism and would leave her needing thyroxine anyway.
key_concept:
TSH direction decides the drug in pregnancy.
  • High TSH (hypothyroid): levothyroxine
  • Already on thyroxine: dose usually needs increasing in pregnancy
  • Low TSH, high T4, first trimester: propylthiouracil
  • Low TSH, high T4, second/third trimester: methimazole/carbimazole
  • Radioactive iodine: never in pregnancy
exam_pearl: Elevated TSH means underactive thyroid; do not reach for an antithyroid drug because the word goiter appears.

stem: 51 year old female k/c of breast cancer on (medication for breast cancer) complaining of abnormal uterine bleeding, she did uterine biopsy and came back inadequate. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
highlight_terms_source: k/c of breast cancer on (medication for breast cancer)
uterine biopsy and came back inadequate
why_right: A 51 year old on breast cancer therapy (classically tamoxifen, which stimulates the endometrium) with abnormal uterine bleeding is at real risk of endometrial hyperplasia or cancer, so a tissue diagnosis is mandatory. When the office biopsy is inadequate, the next step is hysteroscopy with directed biopsy (or D&C), which visualises the cavity and samples focal lesions such as polyps that blind biopsy misses.
why_wrong_block:
A. Reassurance is unsafe: bleeding in a high risk woman with a non diagnostic biopsy has not excluded cancer. It is right only after a benign tissue diagnosis.
C. Hysterectomy without a diagnosis is premature; it is right once cancer or atypical hyperplasia is confirmed (with staging) or for refractory benign disease.
D. Ultrasound is the first test before sampling, but on tamoxifen the endometrium often looks thick and cystic, so it cannot exclude cancer; after an inadequate biopsy in a symptomatic patient tissue is still needed.
key_concept:
AUB work up: never accept a non diagnostic sample in a high risk woman.
  • AUB over 45 years: endometrial biopsy
  • Postmenopausal bleeding: biopsy if endometrium thicker than 5 mm
  • Under 45: biopsy if unopposed estrogen or failed medical therapy
  • Inadequate or negative biopsy with ongoing bleeding: hysteroscopy + directed biopsy/D&C
  • Tamoxifen: raises endometrial cancer risk; any bleeding is investigated
exam_pearl: Inadequate biopsy is not a negative biopsy; escalate to hysteroscopy, do not reassure.

stem: Young woman G maybe 6, has abdominal pain and menorrhagia, she has regular periods every 20 days and lasts 5 days. She has myomectomy 12 years ago and 3 curettage and dilation for abortion. Uterus is bulky and shows no adnexal mass. What is the diagnosis
highlight_terms_source: myomectomy 12 years ago and 3 curettage and dilation
why_right: She has the two classic risk factors for adenomyosis, high parity (G6) and prior uterine surgery (myomectomy and 3 D&Cs), which let endometrium invade the myometrium. Add pain with menorrhagia and a bulky uterus with no adnexal mass, and the picture is adenomyosis.
why_wrong_block:
B. Endometriosis usually leaves a normal sized uterus; it would fit with dyspareunia, infertility, a fixed retroverted uterus, uterosacral nodules or an adnexal chocolate cyst.
C. Fibroids give an irregularly enlarged, firm, non tender uterus with heavy bleeding; they would fit a lumpy uterus on examination rather than a diffusely bulky, painful one.
key_concept:
Adenomyosis = endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium.
  • Risk factors: multiparity, prior uterine surgery (myomectomy, D&C, cesarean)
  • Picture: secondary dysmenorrhea + menorrhagia
  • Exam: diffusely or symmetrically enlarged, boggy, tender uterus
  • Endometrial biopsy is normal (disease is in the myometrium)
  • Treatment: hormonal IUD or OCP; hysterectomy is definitive
exam_pearl: Bulky tender uterus = adenomyosis; irregular firm uterus = fibroids; normal sized uterus with pain = endometriosis.

stem: A 45-year-old P5+3 presented with abnormal uterine bleeding for the last 3 months, regular every 30 days lasting 5 days, with blood clots and pain not relieved by simple analgesia. Previous myomectomy 12 years back and 3 surgical evacuation for incomplete miscarriage. Uterus not palpable abdominally but on pelvic examination bulky and tender with no adnexal mass. BMI 40 kg/m2. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's presentation?
highlight_terms_source: myomectomy 12 years back and 3 surgical evacuation
why_right: A 45 year old P5+3 with previous myomectomy and repeated surgical evacuations has both key risk factors for adenomyosis (multiparity and uterine surgery). Regular heavy periods with clots and pain not relieved by simple analgesia, plus a bulky, tender uterus with no adnexal mass, complete the classic picture.
why_wrong_block:
B. Endometriosis usually has a normal sized uterus; it fits dyspareunia, infertility, fixed retroversion or an endometrioma, none of which is described.
C. Fibroids cause an irregularly enlarged, firm uterus that is usually not tender; the tender, diffusely bulky uterus here points away from them despite the prior myomectomy.
D. Endometrial cancer typically presents as postmenopausal bleeding in an older woman with obesity, diabetes or hypertension; this woman is still cycling regularly with painful clotted periods and a tender uterus. Her BMI of 40 is a real risk factor (so AUB over 45 still warrants endometrial sampling), but it does not explain the picture here.
key_concept:
Bulky tender uterus in a multiparous woman with prior uterine surgery = adenomyosis.
  • Dysmenorrhea + menorrhagia + diffusely enlarged tender uterus
  • Risk factors: multiparity, myomectomy, D&C, cesarean
  • TVUS: myometrial thickening; MRI: thick junctional zone
  • Same picture but postmenopausal with obesity and diabetes: endometrial cancer
exam_pearl: Obesity tempts you toward endometrial cancer, but regular painful cycles in a premenopausal woman keep the answer adenomyosis.

stem: young woman has abnormal uterine bleeding and menorrhagia. That's it. US: normal endometrium. What is the diagnosis
why_right: Heavy menstrual bleeding with a normal endometrium on ultrasound points to disease inside the myometrium: adenomyosis. Ectopic endometrial glands and stroma in the uterine wall cause menorrhagia (often with dysmenorrhea and a diffusely enlarged, boggy uterus), while the endometrial lining itself looks normal, just as an endometrial biopsy is normal in adenomyosis.
why_wrong_block:
A. Endometriosis is ectopic endometrium outside the uterus; it gives dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, dyschezia and infertility with a normal sized uterus, and menorrhagia is not its leading feature.
C. Fibroids cause menorrhagia mainly when submucosal (or large intramural), and ultrasound would show a discrete myometrial or submucosal mass with an irregular, firm enlarged uterus; it would be right if the scan showed such a mass.
key_concept:
Menorrhagia + normal endometrium/biopsy + diffusely enlarged tender uterus = adenomyosis.
  • Adenomyosis: diffuse boggy uterus, menorrhagia + secondary dysmenorrhea; TVUS shows myometrial thickening
  • Fibroid: irregular firm uterus; submucosal type bleeds
  • Endometriosis: normal sized uterus, 3 Ds + infertility
  • Endometrial cancer: postmenopausal, abnormal endometrium on biopsy
  • Risk factors for adenomyosis: multiparity, prior uterine surgery
exam_pearl: Normal endometrium does not exclude a uterine cause; adenomyosis hides in the myometrium, so the lining and biopsy look normal.

stem: Painless vaginal bleeding @35 weeks, patient is stable with reassuring CTG. What is the next step?
key_concept:
Painless bleeding = placenta previa; management depends on bleeding severity, maternal and fetal status, and gestation.
  • Avoid vaginal examination until previa excluded; TVUS localizes the placenta
  • Mode of delivery in previa: cesarean only
  • Stable, mild bleeding: admit, steroids if <34 wk, MgSO4 if <32 wk, planned CS at 36 to 37 wk
  • Severe bleeding or fetal distress at any gestation: stabilize, then emergency CS
  • Painful bleeding + tender uterus = abruption (vaginal delivery possible if stable)
exam_pearl: Stable mother + reassuring CTG + bleeding settled = no rush; the word that flips it to immediate CS is heavy active bleeding or fetal distress.
compiler_note: ⚠ The source marked no answer for this recall (page and next page checked).

stem: A 23-year-old pregnant woman presented with frequency and dysuria for 5 days (see lab result). BP 110/70 mmHg, HR 76/min, Temperature 37.6 °C. Leukocytes 30 (normal 0-3 per high power field). Which of the following is the best treatment option?
why_right: A pregnant woman with frequency, dysuria and pyuria (leukocytes 30/hpf) and only a low grade temperature (37.6 °C, normal BP and HR) has cystitis, which must always be treated in pregnancy. This recall's key is amoxicillin/clavulanate because it is safe throughout pregnancy and covers the usual urinary organisms such as E. coli.
why_wrong_block:
A. Flucloxacillin is an anti staphylococcal penicillin for skin and soft tissue infection (cellulitis, impetigo); it does not reliably cover gram negative urinary pathogens.
C. Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone and is avoided in pregnancy at every stage; it would be right for complicated UTI in a non pregnant adult.
D. Nitrofurantoin is first line for uncomplicated cystitis in non pregnant women; in pregnancy this source treats it as relatively contraindicated (avoid near term, caution in the first trimester), so the key picks a beta lactam instead.
key_concept:
UTI in pregnancy: always treat, and choose a pregnancy safe agent.
  • Safe: amoxicillin/clavulanate, cephalexin (cephalosporins)
  • Avoid at any stage: fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines (doxycycline)
  • Nitrofurantoin: avoid at term (3rd trimester), caution in 1st trimester
  • Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy too
  • Fever, flank pain, vomiting = pyelonephritis: admit for IV antibiotics
exam_pearl: At 38 weeks the same stem keys cephalexin and rejects nitrofurantoin; check the gestational age before choosing nitrofurantoin.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with abnormal uterine bleeding, underwent an endometrial biopsy (see report). Endometrial biopsy: Atypical complex hyperplasia. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: Atypical hyperplasia is premalignant and is definitively treated by hysterectomy, but this patient is "25-year-old", so fertility should be preserved. The fertility-sparing treatment is progestogen therapy (oral progesterone) with close follow-up and repeat endometrial sampling.
why_wrong_block:
A. Tamoxifen has an estrogen-agonist effect on the endometrium and causes hyperplasia; it is never a treatment for it.
B. Hysterectomy is the treatment of atypical hyperplasia when childbearing is complete or in older/postmenopausal women; it would end fertility in a 25-year-old.
D. Endometrial ablation does not treat atypia, destroys fertility and hampers later endometrial surveillance.
key_concept:
Endometrial hyperplasia management depends on atypia and fertility wishes.
  • Without atypia: progestogen therapy
  • With atypia, family complete or older: total hysterectomy
  • With atypia, young or wants fertility: progestogen with follow-up biopsies
  • Diagnosis: endometrial biopsy
  • Risk factors: unopposed estrogen (obesity, PCOS, diabetes, tamoxifen)
exam_pearl: Same biopsy in a 50 or 57 year old flips the answer to hysterectomy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's short version (25 yrs female with atypical complex hyperplasia) highlights Progesterone; fuller Q version answer: C. Oral progesterone.

stem: A 32-year-old pregnant woman at 26 weeks of gestation diagnosed with large genital warts in the vulva. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: In pregnancy (26 weeks) the deciding factor is fetal safety: cryotherapy is a physical ablative method with no systemic absorption, so it is safe at any gestation and is the key here. Most chemical and immunologic wart treatments are avoided in pregnancy.
why_wrong_block:
B. Electrocautery (or surgical excision) is the usual choice for refractory or very bulky warts; it is not the marked answer here because cryotherapy is the simple, pregnancy safe first choice.
C. Podophyllin resin is antimitotic and is absorbed systemically; it is contraindicated in pregnancy (teratogenic and toxic). It is an option only in non pregnant patients.
D. Intralesional interferon is not recommended in pregnancy and is reserved for refractory disease in non pregnant patients; it is not first line anywhere.
key_concept:
Genital warts in pregnancy: physical ablation, not chemicals.
  • Simple wart: cryotherapy (safe in pregnancy)
  • Refractory or large wart: electrocautery / surgical excision
  • Avoid in pregnancy: podophyllin, podophyllotoxin, interferon
  • Warts may grow in pregnancy and regress postpartum
exam_pearl: The word "pregnant" removes podophyllin and interferon at once; between the physical methods, the key goes to cryotherapy.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Compiler's typed options: cryotherapy (highlighted), electrotherapy, podophylline resin, fluconazole. Screenshot also marks **A. Cryotherapy.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with menorrhagia for the last 8 months. She is known to be diabetic and hypertensive. Ultrasound: Thickened endometrial lining of approximately 23 mm. Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value?
OptD: CT of the abdomen and pelvis
why_right: She is 45 with 8 months of menorrhagia, is diabetic and hypertensive (markers of chronic unopposed estrogen exposure), and has a markedly thickened endometrium of "23 mm". Abnormal uterine bleeding at 45 or older is itself an indication for endometrial sampling, and the concern is hyperplasia or carcinoma. Only an endometrial biopsy gives histology, so it has the highest diagnostic value.
why_wrong_block:
B. MRI cannot provide a tissue diagnosis; it is used for local staging once cancer is confirmed.
C. Diagnostic laparoscopy views the peritoneal cavity and outside of the uterus (for example endometriosis) and cannot sample the endometrial cavity.
D. CT is for detecting distant spread and staging, not for diagnosing an endometrial lesion.
key_concept:
Who needs endometrial sampling in AUB.
  • AUB at age 45 or older
  • Under 45 with chronic unopposed estrogen (obesity, PCOS) or AUB failing medical treatment
  • Postmenopausal bleeding with endometrium >5 mm
  • Diabetes, hypertension and obesity raise hyperplasia and cancer risk
  • Imaging (MRI, CT) is for staging after histology
exam_pearl: "Highest diagnostic value" for an endometrial lesion means tissue; imaging only stages.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Option A circled in pen; screenshot Answer: A.

stem: Folic acid dose for pregnant known case of sickle cell disease stable on remission?
why_right: Sickle cell disease causes chronic hemolysis, which depletes folate, so a pregnant woman with SCD needs high dose folic acid throughout pregnancy rather than the standard 0.4 mg. This recall's key is 2.4 mg because it is the only high dose option offered; the textbook high dose is about 4 to 5 mg daily.
why_wrong_block:
A. 0.2 mg is below even the routine preconception dose and is inadequate for any pregnancy.
B. 0.8 mg is close to the average risk dose (0.4 mg) used for women with no added risk; SCD needs a high dose because of ongoing hemolysis.
C. 1.4 mg is still well below the high dose range and is not a recognized regimen; the highest offered option is chosen instead.
key_concept:
Folic acid dose by NTD / folate risk:
  • Average risk: 0.4 mg daily, from at least 1 month before conception
  • High risk (previous NTD, SCD, antiepileptics, diabetes, obesity): high dose, 4 to 5 mg daily
  • SCD: continue high dose throughout pregnancy (hemolysis keeps consuming folate)
  • Hydroxyurea is stopped in pregnancy (teratogenic)
exam_pearl: If 5 mg is listed, pick it; if not, choose the highest dose offered for SCD.

stem: Female with irregular menstrual cycle, she is obese and BMI 31. Labs and blood test are pending.
why_right: An obese woman (BMI 31) with an irregular cycle and labs still pending most likely has a weight related ovulatory disorder such as PCOS. Lifestyle modification (diet and exercise for weight loss) is first line for every such patient: even modest weight loss can restore ovulation and regular cycles, and it is appropriate before any diagnosis is confirmed.
why_wrong_block: B. Combined OCP is the treatment for menstrual irregularity once PCOS is confirmed and pregnancy is not desired; it is added after or alongside lifestyle change, not chosen before workup is complete, and estrogen adds VTE risk in obesity.
key_concept:
PCOS / anovulation management ladder:
  • Step 1 for all: lifestyle modification and weight loss
  • Menstrual irregularity, no pregnancy wish: combined OCP
  • Infertility: ovulation induction (clomiphene or letrozole)
  • Insulin resistance: metformin
  • Hirsutism: OCP, then antiandrogen
exam_pearl: "Labs pending" plus obesity means start with lifestyle; OCP becomes the answer when PCOS is confirmed and the question asks for cycle control.

stem: bhCG Day 1: 1200 mIU/mL; Day 4: 1000 mIU/mL; Day 7: 800 mIU/mL; Day 14: 500. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
OptD: Administer a second dose of methotrexate
why_right: After methotrexate for ectopic pregnancy the decisive comparison is day 4 vs day 7: here 1000 falls to 800, a 20% decline (more than 15%), and it keeps falling to 500 by day 14. This is a successful response, so the plan is to repeat β-hCG weekly until it is undetectable.
why_wrong_block:
A. Ceasing follow up is wrong while β-hCG is still 500; weekly levels must continue until undetectable to exclude persistent trophoblast.
B. Immediate surgery is for rising β-hCG between day 4 and day 7, rupture or hemodynamic instability; levels here are falling steadily.
D. A second methotrexate dose is for a plateau or a fall of less than 15% from day 4 to day 7; here the fall exceeds 15%.
key_concept:
Single dose methotrexate monitoring (compare day 4 with day 7):
  • Fall >15%: weekly β-hCG until undetectable
  • Plateau or fall <15%: second dose of methotrexate
  • Rising: surgical management
  • A rise from day 1 to day 4 is expected and not failure
  • Rupture or instability at any point: surgery
exam_pearl: Ignore day 1; only the day 4 to day 7 change decides between follow up, second dose and surgery.

stem: Pregnant with uncontrolled bleeding resulting in DIC. What is the most common cause?
why_right: Placental abruption is the most common cause of DIC in pregnancy. Retroplacental clot releases tissue factor (thromboplastin) into the maternal circulation, consuming clotting factors and platelets, so bleeding becomes uncontrolled; risk rises with severe or concealed abruption and fetal death.
why_wrong_block:
A. Placenta previa causes painless, often heavy bleeding, but it is a mechanical bleed from the lower segment and rarely triggers DIC.
C. A congenital bleeding disorder (for example von Willebrand disease) can cause pregnancy bleeding but is rare and is not a consumptive coagulopathy.
D. Uterine rupture causes pain, shock and loss of fetal station, usually with prior cesarean or uterotonics; it is far less common than abruption as a cause of DIC.
key_concept:
Obstetric causes of DIC:
  • Most common: placental abruption
  • Others: amniotic fluid embolism, severe pre-eclampsia/HELLP, sepsis, retained dead fetus, massive PPH
  • Abruption: painful bleeding, tender hard uterus, risk factors hypertension, smoking, trauma
  • Previa: painless bleeding, no vaginal exam
exam_pearl: "Pregnant + DIC" defaults to abruption; sudden collapse with hypoxia during labor points to amniotic fluid embolism instead.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Q: restatement (massive uncontrollable vaginal bleeding leading to coagulopathy) also highlights B. Placental abruption.

stem: Patient present with large leiomyoma and menorrhagia prolonged menstruation, see image Hb is 70 What is Most Appropriate Next management Step?
key_concept:
A reference question with this exact scenario is keyed to correct the anemia.
  • Severe anemia from fibroid bleeding: correct anemia first
  • Asymptomatic incidental fibroid: observe, yearly ultrasound
  • Symptomatic: medical first (OCP; GnRH agonist preoperatively to shrink)
  • Large (>7 cm) or failed medical: myomectomy (fertility) or hysterectomy
  • Refuses surgery: uterine artery embolization
exam_pearl: When a low Hb is in the stem and "correct the anemia" is an option, it comes before any fibroid treatment.

stem: Patient present with large leiomyoma and menorrhagia prolonged menstruation, see image Hb is 70 What is Most Appropriate Next management Step?
why_right: This is the variant with no anemia correction option. Among what is offered, the source keys OCP as the next step because symptomatic fibroid bleeding is treated medically first, before uterine artery embolization or surgery, and hormonal control reduces menstrual loss while her anemia is managed.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myomectomy is the fertility sparing surgery for a large fibroid (above about 7 cm) or failed medical treatment; it is not the immediate step in a patient with Hb 70 who has not yet had medical treatment.
B. Uterine artery embolization is reserved for a surgical candidate who refuses surgery; it is not the first line next step.
C. This option is an empty placeholder in the recall; had it said "correct the anemia", that would be the answer (see the sister card).
key_concept:
Fibroid treatment ladder:
  • Severe anemia present: correct anemia first if offered
  • Medical: OCP for symptom control; GnRH agonist before surgery to shrink
  • Surgery for large (>7 cm) or failed medical: myomectomy (fertility) or hysterectomy
  • Refuses surgery: uterine artery embolization
exam_pearl: Same stem, two keys: with an anemia option pick anemia correction; without it, pick medical treatment (OCP) before procedures.
compiler_note: Compiler note: Variant of 1565 where no anemia correction option is given.

stem: A 60-year-old woman is attending the clinic complaining of post-menopausal bleeding for the last 3 months. She was found to have a uterine fibroid of 5 cm in size, noted in a recent ultrasound. Upon review of the previous medical records, the ultrasound performed 5 years ago showed the same size and location of the fibroid. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
why_right: Any post-menopausal bleeding must be evaluated for endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma by endometrial sampling. The fibroid has been the same size and location for 5 years, so it is unlikely to be the new source of bleeding and must not be blamed; a growing fibroid after menopause would instead raise concern for sarcoma.
why_wrong_block:
A. Myomectomy is a fertility-sparing operation for a symptomatic fibroid in a woman who wants children; it is irrelevant at 60 and skips the cancer workup.
B. Hysterectomy may end up being the treatment once histology is known, but operating before tissue diagnosis skips the essential next step and assumes the stable fibroid is the cause.
C. Uterine artery embolization is for symptomatic fibroids in women who decline surgery; it does nothing to exclude endometrial malignancy.
key_concept:
Post-menopausal bleeding = endometrium until proven otherwise.
  • AUB over 45 years: endometrial biopsy
  • Post-menopausal bleeding with thickened endometrium on TVUS: biopsy
  • Stable fibroid on serial imaging: not the culprit
  • Enlarging fibroid after menopause: suspect leiomyosarcoma
exam_pearl: Do not let an old, unchanged fibroid distract you from sampling the endometrium.

stem: Pt had low risk and uncomplicated pregnancy comes for labor. Which of the following is the best intrapartum surveillance to ensure maternal and fetal wellbeing during labor?
OptA: Maternal pulse and blood pressure monitoring
OptC: Early identification of possible labor complications
OptD: Intermittent fetal heart monitoring as it's low risk
why_right: The stem stresses a low risk, uncomplicated pregnancy. For low risk labor, intermittent auscultation of the fetal heart is the recommended fetal surveillance: it is as safe for the baby as continuous CTG and avoids the extra interventions (operative delivery) that continuous monitoring brings without benefit. The question asks for the surveillance that ensures fetal and maternal wellbeing, and fetal heart assessment is the core of that.
why_wrong_block:
A. Maternal pulse and blood pressure are recorded in every labor but say nothing about fetal wellbeing. They become the focus when there is a maternal risk such as hemorrhage or preeclampsia.
B. Contractions are assessed during labor to judge progress, but contraction monitoring alone does not tell you whether the fetus is coping. It is paired with fetal heart assessment, not a substitute for it.
C. Early identification of complications is the goal of intrapartum surveillance, not a surveillance method. It describes why we monitor rather than how.
key_concept:
Fetal heart monitoring method follows risk.
  • Low risk, uncomplicated: intermittent auscultation
  • High risk (FGR/SGA, preeclampsia, diabetes, previous CS, meconium, oxytocin, epidural): continuous CTG
  • Abnormal heart rate on intermittent auscultation: switch to continuous CTG
exam_pearl: Low risk + 'best surveillance' = intermittent auscultation; continuous CTG in low risk labor adds interventions without improving outcome.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-0963B).

stem: A 22-year-old, otherwise healthy woman, presents to the Emergency Room complaining of amenorrhea for the last 8 weeks and expelling blood and tissue through the vagina. Which of the following has the highest diagnostic value?
OptD: Pelvic examination and CT scan of the pelvis
highlight_terms_source: expelling blood and tissue through the vagina
why_right: 8 weeks of amenorrhea with "expelling blood and tissue" means a miscarriage is under way, and the type is defined by two things: whether the cervical os is open or closed and what remains in the uterus. A pelvic (speculum and bimanual) examination assesses the os and any tissue at it, and ultrasound shows retained products or an empty cavity. Together they classify the miscarriage and guide management.
why_wrong_block:
B. Punch biopsy is used for visible cervical lesions and has no role in diagnosing a miscarriage.
C. Abdominal examination cannot assess whether the cervical os is open or tissue is at the os, which is what separates the miscarriage types.
D. CT is not used to evaluate an early pregnancy; it adds radiation and shows uterine contents less well than ultrasound.
key_concept:
Miscarriage type = os status (pelvic exam) + tissue status (ultrasound).
  • Open os, tissue partly passed: incomplete
  • Open os, tissue not passed: inevitable
  • Closed os, all tissue passed: complete
  • Closed os, tissue not passed, non-viable: missed
  • Closed os, viable fetus with bleeding: threatened
exam_pearl: The pelvic exam, not the abdominal exam, tells you if the os is open, which is the fork between miscarriage types.

stem: A 23-year-old primigravida presented at 31 weeks of gestation with preterm labor. Examination revealed, the uterus is contracting and the cervix is closed. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
why_right: This recall's key is magnesium sulfate because at 31 weeks (below 32 weeks) a woman in preterm labor is given MgSO4 for fetal neuroprotection, reducing the risk of cerebral palsy if she delivers. The listed alternatives are tocolytics only and none of them protects the fetal brain. MgSO4 is not chosen for its tocolytic effect, which is weak and not recommended for that purpose.
why_wrong_block:
A. Nifedipine is a first-line tocolytic that can buy time for steroids, but it gives no fetal neuroprotection, which this key prioritizes below 32 weeks.
B. Terbutaline is a beta mimetic with significant maternal side effects (tachycardia, pulmonary edema); it is not first line and has no neuroprotective effect.
C. Indomethacin is a tocolytic option before 32 weeks, but it risks fetal ductus constriction and oligohydramnios and gives no neuroprotection.
key_concept:
Preterm labor drug ladder by gestation.
  • Below 32 weeks: MgSO4 for neuroprotection
  • Below 34 weeks: antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturity (priority if asked for a single drug)
  • Tocolysis (nifedipine, atosiban; indomethacin below 32 weeks) to allow steroids to work
  • GBS prophylaxis antibiotics if delivery expected
exam_pearl: If corticosteroids are among the options below 34 weeks, they take priority over MgSO4.
compiler_note: Repeats: appears 2× in this file (also AS-1969).

stem: A 27-year-old G3 P2 AO L2 at 34 weeks of gestation with severe preeclampsia. Which of the following is the rationale behind giving antihypertensive medications?
OptD: Decrease risk of maternal complications such as stroke
why_right: In "severe preeclampsia" severe-range BP is treated to protect the mother: uncontrolled hypertension causes hemorrhagic stroke, a leading cause of maternal death in preeclampsia. Antihypertensives do not change the placental disease, so they give no proven fetal benefit; delivery is the only cure.
why_wrong_block:
A. Oligohydramnios reflects placental insufficiency; lowering maternal BP does not prevent it.
B. Fetal demise is driven by the underlying placental pathology, which antihypertensives do not reverse; the fetal answer is timely delivery.
C. Growth restriction is not reduced by antihypertensives; overly aggressive lowering may even reduce placental perfusion.
key_concept:
Severe preeclampsia management goals:
  • Antihypertensives → prevent maternal stroke
  • Magnesium sulfate → prevent eclamptic seizures
  • Delivery → definitive cure
  • Steroids if preterm → fetal lung maturity
exam_pearl: Antihypertensives in preeclampsia are for the mother's brain, not the baby.

stem: A 38-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with small for gestational age fetus and reversed end-diastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptC: Antenatal steroids and delivery within 1 week
OptD: Repeat ultrasound growth assessment in 2 weeks
why_right: An SGA fetus with reversed end-diastolic flow (REDV) on umbilical artery Doppler at "33 weeks" is past the gestation at which REDV mandates delivery (32 weeks or more). Surveillance is no longer acceptable, but she is still preterm, so a course of antenatal corticosteroids is given where time allows and delivery is planned promptly afterwards. The key therefore pairs steroids with delivery rather than delivery without steroid cover.
why_wrong_block:
A. Weekly Doppler is routine surveillance for FGR with reassuring results; once REDV appears at 32 weeks or more, waiting a week risks fetal death.
B. Immediate caesarean without steroid cover gives up the neonatal lung benefit of steroids at 33 weeks while the fetus is not yet acutely compromised; immediate delivery is right if CTG or BPP is already abnormal.
D. A growth scan in 2 weeks ignores REDV, the most severe umbilical Doppler finding; growth interval scans suit SGA with normal Doppler.
key_concept:
Umbilical artery Doppler in FGR decides timing.
  • Normal: weekly surveillance, deliver at 37 weeks or more
  • AEDV: deliver at 34 weeks or more; earlier, daily testing
  • REDV: deliver at 32 weeks or more; earlier, daily testing
  • Abnormal CTG or BPP at any stage: deliver
  • Steroids before preterm delivery when time allows; caesarean usually preferred
exam_pearl: REDV below 32 weeks = daily surveillance with steroids; REDV at 32 weeks or more = deliver.

stem: A 38-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with small for gestational age fetus and reversed enddiastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
OptC: Antenatal steroids and delivery within 72 Hours
OptD: Repeat ultrasound growth assessment in 2 weeks
why_right: An SGA fetus with reversed end-diastolic flow on umbilical artery Doppler is the most severe Doppler finding before fetal decompensation, and at 33 weeks (≥32 weeks) the fetus should be delivered rather than monitored. Because she is still preterm (<34 weeks), a course of antenatal corticosteroids is given first to reduce neonatal respiratory distress, with delivery planned promptly afterwards. This recall's key combines both needs: steroids plus delivery within a short window.
why_wrong_block:
A. Weekly Doppler is the surveillance step for FGR with normal or reassuring studies; once REDV appears at ≥32 weeks, waiting a week risks intrauterine death.
B. Delivery is indicated, but at 33 weeks steroids are given first when the fetus is not in acute distress; immediate CS without steroids would be right with a non-reassuring CTG/BPP or maternal instability.
D. A growth scan in 2 weeks ignores the Doppler result; serial growth scans suit an SGA fetus with normal umbilical artery Doppler.
key_concept:
FGR management is driven by umbilical artery Doppler and gestational age.
  • Normal/reassuring: weekly UA Doppler, BPP, NST; deliver at ≥37 weeks
  • Absent EDV: deliver at ≥34 weeks; below that, daily testing
  • Reversed EDV: deliver at ≥32 weeks; below that, daily testing
  • Non-reassuring BPP/NST at any stage: deliver
  • Preterm delivery <34 weeks: give corticosteroids first if time allows
exam_pearl: REDV at ≥32 weeks means deliver, not repeat scanning; the only debate is whether to give steroids first or deliver immediately.
